This research paper focuses on the numerical solution of a stochastic control problem governed by a semilinear heat equation, where the control is applied randomly. Specifically, we are considering the problem of minimizing a cost functional subject to the heat equation with a nonlinear term representing the impact of the control, with the constraint that the control must be nonnegative. To facilitate the analysis, we discretize both space and time variables using the finite element method and the theta-scheme, and establish the convergence of the approximate solution to the optimal solution of the original problem. Notably, when the space of the discretized variable is infinite-dimensional, we derive an estimate of the error term in terms of the discretized parameters. Moreover, we demonstrate the existence and uniqueness of the optimal solution of the continuous problem under weaker conditions than those currently established in the literature. Additionally, we investigate the possibility of adapting the theta-scheme to handle a specific type of nonlinear term. Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of large-scale anisotropy. At the highest energies, we observe an anisotropic excess in specific directionality. Furthermore, we found that the anisotropic component exhibits a distinctive swing in direction as energy increases, from 7.5 to 5.5 EeV. Above 5.5 EeV, the anisotropic excess becomes more pronounced in areas with dense molecular hydrogen content. We also discovered local anisotropy maxima near (l,b) = (339.8deg, -3.9deg) and (306.6deg, -64.2deg), validated by traditional two-sigma excess events as well as machine learning methods. These findings suggest that extremely energetic cosmic rays have origin points or paths that connect them, and that certain areas in the sky become more active during certain periods of the universe's history. The fact that we see these patterns only in the most energetic of cosmic rays suggests that they originate from very distant, possibly universal phenomena, and that we need to examine the intermediate energy range more closely in order to fully understand source directionality. The discovery of these patterns also increases the significance of determining which cosmic rays originate from local sources versus more distant ones, and highlights the importance of continued research in this field. The results presented here will be crucial in guiding future experiments that study extremely energetic cosmic rays, and the potential role that cosmic rays can play in understanding the universe's most powerful phenomena. The findings reported here will be published in a special edition of the journal Physical Review Letters. The lead author of this study is Dr. Alistair C. Smith from the University of Geneva, and the research was conducted in collaboration with members from the Pierre Auger Observatory. Dr. Smith will present the results of this study at the 2020 Polarization, Spin Physics & Non-Standard Searches Workshop, which will be held at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. In evaluating the potential of cancer therapies like immune checkpoint inhibitors, it's crucial to analyze high-resolution images of tumor samples, identifying areas where cancer cells are infiltrated by lymphocytes. This task, known as tumor infiltrating lymphocyte detection, can be complex due to the similarity between cancer and normal tissue. Detection models require large amounts of high-quality data and annotations to be effective, yet such data is hard to acquire. To overcome these challenges, we developed a protocol for the Federated Classification of TILs (FC4TILs) challenge, which allows for the incorporation of annotated data from diverse sources. We pre-trained a lymphocyte detection model and refined it independently in each participating entity using federated learning, with a focus on detecting both central and invasive areas within tumor samples. The challenge consisted of three classification tasks: detecting central-invasive areas, detecting invasive areas, and combining the two as complete invasive areas. The results showed that our approach produced a model performing better than a baseline model trained alone, with a mean AUC of 0.92 for central-invasive area classification, 0.93 for invasive area classification, and 0.94 for the combined task. The code and the challenging protocol are available at https://github.com/strum78/FC4TILs. The challenge demonstrated the potential of federated learning in combining data from diverse sources for medical image classification tasks. The implications of these findings are relevant to any project involving the classification of medical images using multiple entities. The influence of participant selection and the impact of federated learning on models with multiple components were also discussed. The challenge set a precedent for similar approaches in medical research. The opportunity for reducing data requirements through diverse annotations, combined with the findings on participant selection and model components, creates a pathway for the development of more effective, data-efficient models. This paper addresses a significant challenge in underwater fiber communications - the impact of burst errors on decision-feedback equalizers. By demonstrating the considerable distortion caused by burst errors in our field trials, we highlight the limitation of conventional soft-output DF equalizers. To address this issue, we propose an enhanced transmission loss function and adapt the DF equalizer's feedback process to minimize burst errors' adverse effects. With the proposed method, we achieve a notable reduction in bit error rates (BER), surpassing the performance of conventional DF equalizers by at least 2 orders of magnitude in our trial settings. Additionally, our method exhibits comparable computational efficiency to that of conventional DF equalizers. We also explore the optimal selection of transmission losses in relation to SNR in log-scale, leading to a practical approach for adapting DF equalizers in real-time applications. This research focuses on addressing inconsistencies in tabular data sets that contain null values and functional dependencies. By applying a set of corrections to the data, our goal is to minimize the alterations required to eliminate discrepancies while maintaining data integrity. We have developed an algorithm to determine the minimum number of corrections needed to eliminate discrepancies and another one that identifies the optimal set of corrections with the fewest changes. Furthermore, we examined the computational complexity of our problems and proved that one of the optimal solutions has a polynomial complexity in a restricted version. Additionally, we present an effective technique using binary decision trees that can handle larger data sets by introducing a new clustering approach based on data characteristics. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through a performance evaluation using synthetic and real-world data sets. We also discuss potential extensions to our research, including the handling of additional data constraints and the integration of our approach with existing data repair techniques. Count data sequences exhibiting both temporal variation and long-term patterns are common in various fields, characterised by discrete values that reflect the occurrence frequency of events within a set time frame.  Traditional Poisson autoregressive models have been successful in analysing time-invariant data sequences, while more recent designs have accommodated temporal changes through dynamic linking approaches, yet these advancements hold little value without a corresponding framework for forecasting.  To address this limitation, a novel Temporally Varying Poisson Autoregressive (TVPAR) model is developed, capable of handling data sequences with long-term patterns and temporal variations.  A comprehensive framework for estimating TVPAR parameters is established and incorporated into the model, along with a discussion on the likelihood and information matrix of TVPAR estimators.  Meanwhile, the proposed backcasting estimator appears to perform superiorly compared to alternative approaches in simulation settings, while a comparative analysis with dynamic models reveals similarities in the context of the Anzo-Badgo Bridge data.  Notably, the TVPAR model outperforms its dynamic model counterpart in this instance.  To facilitate practical applications, the TVPAR model is implemented in the R package tvpar, featuring a suite of utilities for data preparation, estimation, diagnostics, and forecasting.  The package is made available on the CRAN.  Additionally, a study on the asymptotic distribution of the maximum likelihood estimator and a data example are included in the supplementary materials.  The TVPAR model has the potential to expand the scope of econometric modelling to include multiple regression frameworks.  To this end, researchers are invited to contribute their research based on the proposed TVPAR framework.  Specifically, studies on the generalised TVPAR model and the discrete stochastic frontier analysis model are actively sought.  Anyone interested in collaborating with the researcher on these topics should feel free to reach out and discuss further.  In a related development, a study on the generalised TVPAR model has been submitted for presentation consideration at the upcoming conference.  Meanwhile, the researcher is exploring potential collaborators for the discrete stochastic frontier analysis model study. Through the CAPOS survey, we gathered wide-field observations of this cluster and surrounding field, utilizing optical imaging and infrared photometry to create color-magnitude diagrams and maps of stellar populations. Our data show that Ton 2 exhibits characteristics similar to other rich globular clusters such as Omega Centauri. It contains multiple distinct populations visible in the color-magnitude diagrams and maps. We constructed an isochrone-based selection method to identify members of the second and third generations within Ton 2, and compared these results to previous findings. Our analysis reveals that these multiple populations follow the same radial distribution within the cluster. We also detected a slight gradient in the metallicity of Ton 2's multiple populations, with [Fe/H] ranging from -0.67 to -0.56. Our analysis of the horizontal branch morphology suggests that Ton 2 undergoes slight non-adaptive thermal pulses, which is consistent with predictions for clusters of this magnitude. Our data show that the radial velocity of Ton 2 is 54.01 ± 0.19 km/s, and we discovered three distinct absorption features in our data, matching the frequencies of two previously identified moving groups. We analyzed the chemical composition of Ton 2's multiple populations, revealing distinct [α/Fe] ratios, with [α/Fe] ranging from 0.31 to 0.38. Our analysis of elemental abundances revealed variations in the levels of oxygen, magnesium, and carbon across the cluster, with enhanced abundances found in the second and third generations. We discovered a correlation between these elements and the cluster's radial velocity, and our data show that Ton 2 exhibits a slight deficit of nitrogen. Our analysis of elemental abundances within Ton 2 follows the typical pattern observed in other rich globular clusters, consistent with theories of stellar feedback in the early universe. Our data show that Ton 2 exhibits a slight deficit of s-process elements, and our analysis of [N/α] ratios revealed variations across the cluster, with enhanced nitrogen found in the second and third generations. Our analysis of these elemental abundances shed light on the complex formation history of this cluster, involving multiple interactions between Ton 2 and nearby field stars. We constructed an analytical model replicating the chemical composition of Ton 2's multiple populations, and our predictions matched observed data. The Yang-Lee edge (YLE) critical behavior represents a phenomenon where Yang-Lee zeros shift from the real axis to the complex plane, and its classification into universality classes (UCCs) has been a subject of study for many years. Although significant progress has been made, determining the global position of the YLE critical point within the O(N) universality classes remains an open question. In this study, we explore this issue by examining the scaling laws that govern both the Yang-Lee edge and bulk critical behaviors, and by analyzing the relationships between the YLE's central charge and specific heat exponents from both the edge and bulk perspectives. Our findings indicate that the YLE's central charge exhibits unique values that differ from those of the corresponding bulk phase, and our proposed classification system offers a framework that unifies previous results, filling gaps in the O(N) universality class chart. Additionally, our research identifies new universal exponents for both the YLE and bulk critical behaviors within the O(N) universality class chart. Our theoretical models also suggest that the YLE critical behavior may occur within a more expansive universality class than previously thought, and we anticipate that many systems will display this more extensive universality, as supported by numerical data from Ising and O(3) models. Our research focuses on static variables, and further investigation is needed to clarify the status of the YLE within dynamical O(N) universality classes. Our work contributes significantly to the understanding of critical phenomena within O(N) universality classes. In statistics and machine learning, it is frequently essential to establish whether a basic optimization method on a non-convex function can eventually enter a region where the function becomes locally convex. To address this, we developed an inequality that enables us to analyze the properties of the optimization landscape surrounding the solutions produced by an approximate message passing (AMP) algorithm. Specifically, we applied our inequality to demonstrate the local convexity of a particular TAP free energy function, which is relevant to the Z2 synchronization problem and the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model. Additionally, our inequality led to a confirmation of a previous conjecture regarding the efficiency of a sampling algorithm in the "easy" regime of these models. Furthermore, our inequality can be used to prove the correctness of a previous prediction regarding the performance of the AMP algorithm in the "hard" regime of these models, particularly under the condition that the number of variables in each cluster is significantly greater than the number of clusters. 

In the context of the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model, our inequality led to a novel proof of the correctness of a previous prediction regarding the performance of the AMP algorithm in the "easy" regime, without relying on the previous arguments involving the Gaussian vector model.

While using stellar photometry to study the interstellar medium is common, there is a need to move beyond qualitative results due to the precision of modern photometric data. This study presents a novel method to accurately measure the interstellar medium's dust characteristics and the scattering matrix over a specific wavelength range, despite being restricted to narrow bands available from stellar photometry. By applying this approach to multiple stars, we obtained a comprehensive dataset that includes six distinct directions across the galaxy and six different direction combinations. Our findings show that dust behaves uniformly across the galaxy and that our method is sensitive enough to detect small changes in dust characteristics, especially in the blue-to-violet range. Additionally, we discovered that dust scatters additional energy at approximately 4200 A, consistent with laboratory measurements of large microparticles. Our study also found that dust plays a significant role in scattering light in the violet-to-ultraviolet range and that our model fails to accurately capture this phenomenon when directions are more sideway. This study's results have implications for interpreting data from future missions that will study the interstellar medium and the intergalactic medium by analyzing light that has been scattered in different directions. However, if the object's appearance lacks distinct features, additional information is necessary to calculate the pose in a single image. We address this challenge by introducing an end-to-end deep learning method called DeepHMap++ that utilizes a merged projection of two images to calculate the pose for non-robust objects. We also present a new dataset called DavisPlus to facilitate research on this problem. Our investigation compares DeepHMap++ to a baseline approach that consists of a separate correspondence learning step. The results show that DeepHMap++ achieves enhanced clustering accuracy and significantly outperforms the baseline in terms of pose calculation error. Furthermore, we find that pose calculation accuracy can reach 45 degrees of freedom (DoF) on a DavisPlus dataset with clustered features, surpassing the baseline's 36 DoF. Bond-oriented peridynamics has emerged as a particular approach within this framework, effectively handling the modeling of fluid materials by utilizing nonlocal constitutive functions. This framework has been applied to various problems including potential theory, surface-tension effects, and phase-transition dynamics. Furthermore, Bond-oriented peridynamic equations have been derived from the Hamilton principle, providing a comprehensive understanding of the approach. Although Bond-oriented peridynamics has primarily been utilized to model material phenomena, researchers have explored the potential of extending this approach to field theories, such as General Relativity. However, significant challenges remain in applying Bond-oriented peridynamics to model fluid materials, mainly due to the absence of a constitutive theory. Nonetheless, this review showcases the potential of Bond-oriented peridynamics to unify local and nonlocal theories of mechanics within a consistent mathematical framework. Due to its conceptual sophistication, this review is targeted at an advanced audience with expertise in applied mathematics and physics. Key concepts within this review, including Bond-oriented peridynamics, Hamiltonian mechanics, and Hamilton-Oliver rational nonlinearity, are clearly defined for the reader's convenience. We present GGLasso, a Python-based library that computes key matrix estimators under the Generalized Graphical Lasso framework, incorporating experts' prior knowledge through $\ell_1$ constraints. Numerous applications in physics, chemistry, and materials science frequently hinge on modeling molecular systems for optimal configuration. This often requires efficiently sampling configurational space. Although various dynamical methods are utilized for this purpose, we demonstrate that a straightforward application of velocity verlet with a significant step size can be highly effective. By analyzing model systems, we show that this method not only rivals more complex algorithms like Nos\'e-Hoover and Hoover, but in some cases surpasses them in terms of configuration sampling efficiency. Moreover, we explore how the velocity verlet method's performance is influenced by system size, temperature, and friction constants. Our findings suggest that this simple approach can be an easy way to achieve superior configurational sampling. We also examine the velocity verlet method's conservation properties and discuss its connection to more complex thermodynamic cycles. This study is particularly relevant to nanoscale systems and we anticipate it will be useful for researchers working with molecular systems over short to medium-sized time scales. In such cases, we expect that velocity verlet will be a superior choice over other methods. In addition, we believe that this study will be pertinent to a wider audience of scientists who are familiar with dynamical methods but may not necessarily be experts in molecular dynamics. We further analyze that the velocity verlet method's advantages could be understood from an electromechanical perspective, which we discuss in detail. This study is a follow-up to our earlier work on pulsed friction, and we demonstrate that the velocity verlet method can be seen as a variant of pulsed dynamics that is specifically tailored for configurational sampling. We anticipate that this study will be of interest to a broader audience of scientists who are working on model systems and are familiar with dynamical methods. We examine the extended Euler-Bernoulli beam equation on a star-shaped graph consisting of a central hub with n connected branches. The corresponding boundary value problem is established and specific boundary conditions are defined to stabilize the system in a normed Hilbert space. The critical part of the problem is then shown to be a topological degenerate Fredholm operator of index one. By applying a Lopitza-Minty theorem, we find a specific boundary condition that makes the operator A strongly positive. This condition is composed of the sum of the boundary flexural rigidity and a specific fractional power of the Laplacian on each branch being nonnegative. As a result, we derive the existence and uniqueness of solutions to the boundary value problem and establish its stability. Additionally, we prove that A generates a compact accumulation operator on the C-space and multiple rotating modes of the beam exist. Finally, we verify the asymptotic stability of the system by applying the Houston-Simonis boundary condition, which is compatible with physical principles. This research is an extension of previous studies on the Euler-Bernoulli equation on a star-shaped graph. Specifically, it generalizes the existing theory to include the beam's rotational kernel. The associated resolvent boundary condition is introduced and shown to lead to the compact accumulation property of the operator A, which in turn guarantees the asymptotic stability of the system. This conclusion is demonstrated through the application of the Houston-Simonis boundary condition, which preserves the symmetry of the boundary data. Additionally, we establish the existence and uniqueness of solutions to the boundary value problem and prove the strong stability of the system by analyzing the operator A's fractional powers and the compact accumulation property. This research expands the existing theory to include the rotational Euler-Bernoulli equation on a star-shaped graph and provides a more general framework for the study of coupled partial differential equations on graph structures. To address this, we introduce a novel approach that treats the detection of all entities as a single integrated task, rather than a sequential one. By analyzing the text as a whole, our method leverages both local and global features to build a comprehensive entity structure, which guides the classification of each entity based on its position within this structure. Specifically, our system achieves an F-score of 92.75% for nested entities, outperforming existing state-of-the-art models by a 0.75% point improvement. This study tackles the challenge of solving a specific mathematical problem related to the optimization of organic conic formulations, specifically those expressed in the format of semidefinite programs with matrix-valued functions representing various structures, such as positive semidefinite matrices, copositive matrices, and skew cone structures. Building on the foundation of existing research, we develop a general method for converting certain organic conic formulations into equivalent problems that can be solved using specialized solvers for semidefinite programs, such as SDPA. We also introduce a new open-source Julia package called Hypatia, which provides an efficient and user-friendly interface for users to work with matrix-valued functions and related structures. With Hypatia, users can easily determine if a given positive semidefinite constraint is feasible, and if not, can obtain a factorization of the matrix that represents the structure. We further extend the capabilities of Hypatia to handle more complex structures, such as copositive and skew cone structures. We then show how Hypatia can be used to solve general organic conic formulations efficiently, and provide an update on the current performance of the Hypatia package. Finally, we encourage other researchers to explore the potential of combining algorithmic techniques and structural properties to develop more efficient solution algorithms for organic conic formulations. We also include a demonstration of the Hypatia package by applying it to a specific formulation related to skew cone structures, and provide an updated version of the package that addresses some of the performance issues. We believe that the Hypatia package has the potential to become a leading solver for organic conic formulations in the future. We also plan to continue working on several open research questions related to the Hypatia package, and we hope that this study will attract the interest of other researchers in the field. The Intel Optane DC Persistent Memory Module (DC PMM) has reached commercial viability as a main memory technology. It offers fast, large-capacity storage that distinguishes itself from traditional solid-state drives. Optane DC PMM enables data to remain accessible during power outages and reduces storage needs by minimizing the memory-to-storage ratio. However, its performance characteristics vary depending on the system and use case. In this work, we convey the practical performance benefits achievable with Optane DC PMM in data centers and cloud computing environments. We examine four application scenarios - database management, web serving, cloud storage, and scientific simulation - and report on the performance gains and losses resulting from various configuration approaches. Our findings show that Optane DC PMM can accelerate application performance by a factor of three in the most favorable cases and still experiences performance regressions due to various issues. In order to lower the main memory costs, we investigate the effects of reducing the memory-to-storage ratio and show that certain applications can tolerate a 4x decrease in memory without performance degradation, while others continue to experience performance losses even at the lowest tested ratio. Finally, we explore the implications of energy and cooling cost savings resulting from reduced memory requirements and estimate the potential annual cost savings for a data center-scale deployment. Our research demonstrates that energy-efficient energy and cooling cost savings can be achieved with Optane DC PMM across multiple application scenarios and usage configurations. In particular, our analysis indicates that cloud workloads and applications that tolerate low memory-to-storage ratios can experience significant annual cost savings with Optane DC PMM. In contrast, databases and scientific applications may require further optimization or alternative solutions before they can take full advantage of the energy and cooling cost savings provided by low memory-to-storage ratios. In the context of cloud computing, our research highlights the potential for significant annual cost savings with Optane DC PMM, especially when combining it with cost-effective virtual machine sizing, which can lead to substantial reductions in memory requirements. In this scenario, our study shows that Optane DC PMM can result in annual cost savings of up to $1.7 million for a data center-scale deployment. The foundation theorem in combinatorics, initially applied to the Coxeter group of type A, specifies that any element within a Coxeter group whose Weyl length reflects its distance to the identity, can be expressed as a reduced word. We investigated the metallic phase of LaNiO$_3$ using $^8$Li $\beta$-detected NMR in LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattices with varying nickel oxide layer thickness. Our spin-lattice relaxation studies in a 6.55 T magnetic field yielded T$^1$ recovery curves in temperatures ranging from 50 K to 300 K, revealing different behavior in two temperature ranges. At higher temperatures, a relatively fast spin-lattice relaxation rate allowed for accurate spin temperature determination, while at lower temperatures, it became insufficient due to spin flip recovery. In the higher temperature range, we observed a proportional relationship between the square of the spin lattice relaxation rate and temperature, indicative of a spin fluctuation mechanism. Additionally, we observed a pronounced shift in the Knight shift at higher temperatures, which we attribute to a population shift caused by electronic transitions across the LaNiO$_3$ energy gap. Our results provide valuable insights into the electronic properties of LaNiO$_3$, a material where the sole magnetic interaction is expected to be long-range Heisenberg coupling. Notably, we find that this expected ground state may be avoided by incorporating LaAlO$_3$ layers through interface effects that likely introduce antiferromagnetic next-nearest-neighbor interactions, thus favoring a more stable Néel state. Furthermore, we discuss possible implications of these findings on the material's phase diagram and the role of strain and interface effects in controlling the electronic and magnetic properties of LaNiO$_3$. Our study also highlights the utility of $^8$Li $\beta$-detected NMR as a means to study the electronic properties of LaNiO$_3$ and other correlated oxides. We anticipate that this technique will contribute substantially to the advancement of theoretical models of these materials' electronic structures. Specifically, our dataset comprises detailed information on 18 aspects of physiology and biology, including eight traits whose genetic predispositions have been thoroughly explained, 7 complex disorders influenced by multiple genetic factors, and 3 characteristics primarily determined by a single gene. Notably, our dataset includes functional genomic data on over 18 million distinct genetic elements across 125 species of model organisms, along with comprehensive genome-wide association study data on all 18 characteristics. Our team has used this comprehensive dataset to examine the functional implications of genetic variations associated with these characteristics and has made the results available in an interactive dashboard available online. By incorporating vast amounts of genomic and association study data, we have a fundamental understanding of how genetic variations influence these characteristics at a functional level. Additionally, our analysis has pinpointed potential connections between these characteristics that are supported by genetic evidence and has identified key genetic factors contributing to each of the 18 aspects of physiology and biology. Moreover, our analysis has revealed significant links between these characteristics that are supported by genetic evidence, such as the fact that genetic variations associated with an increased risk of disease also contribute to a higher altitude tolerance, while genetic variations that lower tolerance for extreme temperatures also decrease tolerance for humidity. Our analysis has provided a comprehensive understanding of the genetic mechanisms underlying these characteristics, and we believe that our approach can be applied to gain a deeper understanding of the genetic mechanisms underlying any characteristic influenced by genetic variations. Observations of certain variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center have revealed that they exhibit extremely long intervals between repetitions of the same spectral patterns, ranging from half a century to several decades.  The vast majority of these sources are located in close binaries and are thought to have a companion star with mass either low enough to avoid significant mass loss or high enough to have already absorbed the star's material, causing it to collapse into a black hole.  The absence of any notable outflows from these sources has led to their being classified as dormant neutron star binaries or low-mass dormant black hole binaries.  The length of repetition intervals for these sources does not follow any well-defined patterns related to the sources' luminosities or locations within the galaxy.  However, it has been found that the X-ray binaries with shorter repetition intervals contain a neutron star while the ones with longer intervals contain a black hole, which would provide these sources with a mechanism for controlling the pace of their observations.  The absence of any significant outflows from these sources makes it difficult to use this method and instead consideration should be given to using the repetition intervals themselves, which demonstrate a clear distinction between the sources containing a neutron star and those containing a black hole, allowing for an inference about the status of the recently discovered highly persistent X-ray source, GC X-4, which is also a close binary.  This inference suggests that GC X-4's spectrum belongs to an intermediate persistence class and its repetition interval is likely linked to its current persistent state, which in turn implies the presence of a accretion disk in this source, making GC X-4's nature as an intermediate persistence variable neutron star binary transient.  Furthermore, GC X-4's location within the galaxy, combined with the fact that its repetition interval falls within the range of the known solitary neutron star transients, supports the theory that GC X-4 is an isolated neutron star located at a distance of approximately 8.5 kiloparsecs from the Earth.  The fact that GC X-4 is not located near any known massive star within its surrounding 10 parsecs also supports this distance measurement, which in turn implies that GC X-4 is more likely than previously thought to be a member of the old population present in the galaxy's center.  Finally, GC X-4's repetition interval is expected to shorten as it transitions from its current persistent state, making it likely that this source will soon exhibit the same bright outflows that are typically seen in the galaxy's center's transient

We explore the impact of waves generated by massive stellar explosions on their surrounding envelopes, analyzing how they interact with each other and affect the overlying tissue. Focusing on the case where a strong forward-directed shock wave emerges, we observe that it may survive to significant distances from the star, influencing its surroundings through multiple interactions. By analyzing various modes of energy transfer, we identify that radiative losses associated with the shocks contributing to mass loss, while other processes such as conductive heating and fast hadron decay contribute minimally due to their low efficiency. Furthermore, we find that waves with longer wavelengths dominate the energy release at later stages, often resulting in the generation of stronger shocks when compared to short wavelength waves that are damped more quickly. This distinction allows for a simpler model predicting wave behavior, which highlights the importance of stellar physics, especially in the formation of forward-directed shocks, as well as massive stars having the potential to produce fast hadron decay due to their longer lifetime. This research provides a foundation for examining wave behavior in general and sheds light on the potential for fast hadron decay in multiple stellar phenomena, such as massive eruptions and supernovae. We undertake a comprehensive analysis of a class of virtual electronic interactions that are dependent on momentum and ubiquitous in digital technologies. These interactions cause a range of subtle effects, including the manipulation of spin-orbit coupling, variation of band structure, and activation of specific velocities, all of which are essential for optimal electronic device performance. To illustrate this, we examine piezoelectric quantum wells under stress, revealing a complex spectrum of electrons that interact with each other and vibrational fields in multiple ways. This insight applies broadly to any digital system comprising electrons and vibrational fields and provides a foundation for the exploration of more complex phenomena arising from higher-order interactions. By modeling a strained graphene system, we demonstrate that the effects of electron-vibrational and spin-vibrational interactions can be circumvented, allowing for the realization of ideal, two-level systems. Nevertheless, in digital technologies, these interactions often cannot be disregarded, leading to the coherent exchange of energy between electrons, vibrational fields, and the generation of new, long-lived states. Furthermore, these effects can be manipulated to enhance specific interactions, field activations, or to create temporary modifications in the electronic landscape, all of which can be achieved through simple adjustments to the stress applied to the material. This, in turn, enables a level of optimization that, when combined with momentum-dependent interactions, can produce a crucial level of performance in digital technologies that cannot be achieved otherwise. As such, digital technologies that rely on electrons and vibrational fields will always require a stress factor and cannot be fully understood through theoretical models that ignore this influence. We stress that this analysis holds a general validity, applicable to any digital technology whatsoever, regardless of its specific technology profile. In conclusion, we propose that research into the consequences of stress should be a central focus in the study of digital technologies, given its universally impactful nature. This framework combines elements of both scenarios, applying general relativistic principles to a relativistic jet and accounting for the expansion of a wide range of jet cones, from narrow to full spheres. By integrating the dynamics of both shock types, the authors derive a set of consistent equations that describe the evolution of both internal and external shock temperatures, as well as the dynamics of fireballs and jets. Additionally, this framework enables a more comprehensive identification of both internal and external shock components from observational data, including temperature, density, and radius of both the fireball and jet cones. Additionally, this framework may offer a better explanation for cases where late-time afterglow observations diverge from traditional expectations. We have investigated multiple approaches to incorporate calibration techniques in imbalanced incremental learning processes. Our experiments revealed that both online and offline calibration strategies can enhance the performance on batch datasets, with online methods showing superior results. Moreover, our study discovered that employing the same network for classification and calibration is not necessarily the most effective approach. We observed that utilizing a separate network for calibration can result in improved performance, with this benefit being more pronounced in scenarios involving highly unbalanced datasets. Our research provided valuable insights on the application of calibration techniques in the complex scenario of visual data stream learning and we expect these findings to contribute to future development of new algorithms. This class inherently includes all real closed fields and provides an equivalent formulation for the class of globally stable fields first introduced by Giusti. Our work involves an investigation of fields that are both respected and complete in relation to their residue map, considering their geometric and algebraic aspects. This leads to an identification of the algebraic structure associated with RWCFs as a finite extension of the rational function field over a set of RWCFs via a specific map. This structure is shown to be applicable across an infinite number of dimensions. Furthermore, we establish a connection between RWCFs and globally stable fields through an example of the latter field to demonstrate its relationship to a specific RWCF, followed by an examination of the possible values of the geometric norm associated with a globally stable field. This analysis enables us to prove that certain globally stable fields can be constructed as a finite extension of the ground field, and conversely, that some respected fields with a complete residue map are globally stable fields. Additionally, we explore RWCFs within the context of nonarchimedean analysis and show that fields of the type F((t^N)), where F is a respected field and t is an indeterminate, are RWCFs for any positive integer N. This construction, however, fails for N=1. Our work also involves the demonstration of a specialized version of the Stone-Weierstrass theorem for RWCFs, along with an examination of the continuity of the geometric norm associated with globally stable fields. This continuity holds if and only if the ground field is a subfield of the field of respect. We further investigate the relationship between the geometric norm and the standard norm for fields of the type F((t^N)) and show that they coincide exactly when N is an even number. This analysis enables us to establish an exact condition under which the standard norm associated with a respected field with a complete residue map is continuous. This condition is met when the field of respect is a subfield and this results in the continuity of the standard norm for a specific class of globally stable fields. Recent studies demonstrating effective side-channel resistance through degradation of computational performance are primarily limited to low-level programming frameworks. However, applications often utilize higher-level programming languages for efficiency. This work delves into the possibility of achieving side-channel manipulation at the operating system level, specifically on a range of Linux-based systems. We examine various OS-related factors that influence performance manipulation, which can be manipulated in certain cases, allowing for the development of applications utilizing higher-level programming languages that can evade modern side-channel attacks. This is exemplified through the creation of a shell command that raises errors on certain inputs, thus diverting program execution between two distinct performance paths, thereby evading a specific type of attack. This technique can be applied across multiple types of Linux-based systems, including mobile and web-based applications. The approach is then expanded upon to address potential drawbacks, such as the need for explicit error checking by programmers, which could potentially compromise the effectiveness of the strategy. The revised solution focuses on unconscious exploitation of performance degradation, where programs are intentionally designed to experience delays, which can be misleading to certain types of attacks. This new approach is shown to provide side-channel quiet performance, reducing output data by a factor of a hundred, while maintaining a significant increase in system throughput, up to twenty times. This is further demonstrated through the development of several practical applications utilizing this technique, which includes the creation of a silent version of the memcached service, which can be used as a web-based attack tool, a side-channel quiet version of the Redis service, which can be used as a real-time web-based cache service, and a silent version of the Twain, an image scanner interface, which can be used as a real-world input device. These developed applications can provide a high level of security against certain types of attacks by hiding performance variations, which could otherwise be utilized by an attacker, providing a useful solution for developing side-channel attack-free applications. This work also explores the possibility of obtaining optimal performance from CPU execution, which can be achieved through the manipulation of CPU instruction codes, allowing for the evading of certain types of attacks by reordering execution, at a cost of up to thirty percent more time. Based on unitarity principles, we found that a solution to the anomaly could imply the presence of New Physics at an energy scale of roughly 10-18 TeV, which could potentially be as low as 5 TeV if the Higgs' interaction with the W and Z bosons is in line with Standard Model predictions. This outcome may have the added benefit of significantly increasing the rate of di-Higgs production in future muon colliders. Ultimately, this study underscores the importance of precisely measuring the Higgs coupling to a muon and itself in forthcoming experiments.

This approximation holds when the frequency range is narrow in comparison to the frequency spacing between modes. By selecting an appropriate frequency range that minimizes crosstalk, we can create balanced inputs capable of producing frequency-resistant Molmer-Sorensen gates. The effectiveness of this method is illustrated through simulations of ion trap implementations, where applying balanced inputs results in nearly uniform performance across various frequency ratios, in contrast to the typical variation seen with uniform single-mode rotations. This protocol is also shown to significantly improve the efficacy of Molmer-Sorensen gates in scenarios with large frequency deviations, such as in applications involving multiple ion traps. The execution of this gate is made possible by utilizing a combination of frequency-selective Fock-state preparations and symmetric initial motional states, which together allow the exploitation of cross-talk effects to create robust gate performance. In the context of time series modeling, real-world applications often involve forecasting scenarios that are then used for broader statistical analysis purposes. Given this, it's common for financial and economic time series to be forecasted. In this area of study, linear models have been highly effective tools for forecasting and modeling correlated data sets. Given the popularity of least squares estimation, it's widely used for model fitting. However, the standard least squares estimator is sensitive to issues arising from non-stationarity and differencing operations within time series data sets, resulting in biased estimates and a failure to meet usual assumptions. In this research, we examine the performance of least squares estimation when used on time series data sets that have been linearly transformed, focusing specifically on the situation where models are fit to differenced data sets. We show that under specific conditions, the standard asymptotic theory for least squares estimation applies, even in the presence of non-stationarity and differencing. Furthermore, we investigate the situation where models are fit to forecasting scenarios involving overlapping blocks of data sets, also deriving the asymptotic distribution of the estimator in this case. The results are then validated through the use of simulation studies, before being applied to a real-world data set related to economics. The findings of this research hold significant value for researchers and practitioners of time series research, as it identifies the circumstances under which standard linear models can be applied to time series data sets successfully. The research contributes to the expansion of the general time series framework, allowing linear models to be applied to a wider range of data sets, including those that have been linearly transformed. The research takes an important step in unifying the standards of time series models, making it easier to compare the performance of different models. In quantum physics, decomposition of an electron wave function into its components plays a vital role in understanding molecular and atomic behavior, particularly when probed by extreme-ultraviolet light. This process is usually investigated using photoelectron spectra, but recent advancements in x-ray free-electron lasers have created new opportunities for studying electron dynamics triggered by intense x-ray pulses. To fully exploit these possibilities, a new framework called Auger-Meitner decomposition (AMD) has been developed to analyze interference patterns in electron wave functions. This framework combines elements of single-electron states, interference patterns, and parentage coefficients to accurately explain effects observed in the time-domain. Theoretical models, such as mean-field and multielectron dynamics simulations, can be used to interpret interference patterns and retrieve the time-dependent occupation probabilities of single-electron states. However, these models typically assume the existence of well-defined single-electron states, which may not hold in certain situations, particularly in systems with strong correlations. As a result, there is a need for a more comprehensive decomposition that considers the entire electron system, which has never been directly observed in an interference pattern. By manipulating the rotation periods of artificially generated planets and observing the resulting effects on atmospheric circulation, our research aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the interactions between planetary conditions and atmospheric phenomena. According to our findings, fast Rotating Planets (FRPs) with short rotation periods exhibit cyclostrophic super-rotation, characterized by wind patterns rotating faster than the planet itself, while medium Rotating Planets (MRPs) with medium rotation periods show geostrophic balance and experience turbulent mixing, and Slow Rotating Planets (SRPs) with extended rotation periods display little to no turbulence. Additionally, we discovered that MRPs offer the ideal environment for studying planetary-scale turbulence and that varying the planetary temperature in this range does not significantly impact atmospheric circulation patterns. The vast disparity between training and inference costs for large-scale neural networks stems from unnecessary computational complexity resulting from redundant batch dimensions. Our proposed approach, Dynamic Learning at the ImageNet Magnitude (DLNM), circumvents this issue by simplifying batch dimensions during training. DLNM achieves this by limiting the dimensionality to $K$ ($K\leq32$) through the application of average pooling and a learned hyperbolic tangent activation function. Our findings indicate that models trained via DLNM on the ImageNet dataset exhibit comparable performance to their fully batched counterparts, while reducing training and inference costs by a factor of 4 and 3 respectively. Moreover, our method facilitates more efficient inference by introducing a startup factor related to the average of the squared magnitudes of each layer's weights, which can be mitigated over time through additional training. We validate our approach by achieving comparable performance to state-of-the-art methods on the CIFAR-100 dataset, with a significant reduction in training and inference costs. The code for our method has been made publicly available on the DeepLearnCode Repository and the DisBatch Learning at the ImageNet Magnitude Repository. Additionally, our models trained via DLNM on the ImageNet dataset have been made publicly available on the ImageNet DisBatch Learn Repository. We have also introduced an open-access dataset, the Small Dataset DisBatch Learn Repository, which comprises disbatched versions of multiple smaller datasets. Our results suggest that models trained via DLNM exhibit better performance on larger images, achieving an accurate classification score of 0.294 on the VOC2009 dataset, whereas the current state-of-the-art super-resolution model yields a score of 0.294 on the VOC2009 dataset, albeit at a significantly higher computational cost. Both theoretical modeling and experimental results revealed the convergence of two conduction bands in the center of HgTe trenches, leading to helical edge states that possess unique symmetry. The absence of a bandgap in these structures necessitates a consideration of interaction between the harnessing and barrier regions, which however does not significantly affect the quantum Hall state. Notably, the edge state conductivity exhibits insulating behavior when subjected to a perpendicular magnetic field. This study investigates hall irregularity in fixed-lattice vortices within the boundary layer of a type II superconductor using a precise computational method. We employed a numerical approach to analyze thin-film data from BSCCO and compared the results to a simplified theoretical model, discovering that the hall irregularity can be understood through a specific value, the square of which follows a direct relationship with temperature in the superconductor's normal state. This relationship leads to a precise definition of high and low temperature regimes in the normal state, separated by a critical temperature that is linear with the square of the applied magnetic field strength. Notably, this critical temperature matches the onset temperature of the superconducting phase for low applied magnetic fields. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the hall irregularity value follows a non-linear, direct relationship with the applied magnetic field strength in the superconductor's normal state. We also propose a new theoretical model that accounts for hall irregularity in the normal state, and our results suggest that this phenomenon is a manifestation of a persistent critical current flow in the superconductor's normal state. This concept is supported by a separate study on the superconductor's dynamic response. Ultimately, our research provides a clear understanding of hall irregularity in the normal state, and we anticipate that this knowledge will be valuable to the scientific community. In the Ising model, the second moment of the magnetization naturally leads to a higher-order correlation that can be used to determine a magnetic induction parameter. This interaction causes a shift in the critical exponent of the magnetization and creates a new universal fixed point in the 3D Ising universality class. We investigate this fixed point and show that it is stable along a specific trajectory in the 3D Ising universality landscape, which can be explored using Monte Carlo simulations in the absence of an external field. We find that the magnetic induction parameter leads to a specific scaling of the specific heat and susceptibility near the critical point, and that it causes a shift in the critical exponents of these quantities by approximately 0.25 in dimensions other than three. We also measure the critical amplitudes of the magnetization, susceptibility, and specific heat in the presence of long-range correlations and find them to be consistent with predictions made by the universal jump model. We provide an exact relation for the free energy near the critical point, which confirms the predicted scaling of the specific heat and allows us to measure the Casimir amplitude, which is consistent with expectations based on the universal jump model. We conclude that the fixed point of the 3D Ising model, which arises from the fourth moment of the magnetization, is indeed a fundamental component of the universal physics near the critical point and that it may play a crucial role in understanding non-universal behavior observed in recent experiments. In recent years, advancements in X-ray technology and training algorithms have revolutionized the detection of prohibited items. Nonetheless, achieving high-performance banned items identification remains a complex challenge. A significant obstacle lies in the abundance and varied forms of commonplace objects that can mask prohibited items, thereby hindering detection. Existing benchmarks and evaluation methods for X-ray-based prohibited items identification are limited to specialized datasets and cultural contexts, thereby constraining the applicability of developed models to real-world scenarios. Moreover, a lack of horizontal attention mechanisms in convolutional neural networks has been a major limitation, as they can suppress contextual information and impair the performance of these models. To address these shortcomings, we present a novel horizontal attention lateral suppression module that incorporates a horizontal attention mechanism to extract local features and a lateral suppression module to integrate contextual information from adjacent regions. This custom module is incorporated into a baseline detector, and in conjunction with an optimized dataset, yields a score of 0.8142 on the evaluation server. This represents a notable improvement of 0.1275 over the current state-of-the-art on the custom Real-World X-ray Valuation Dataset and surpasses the performance of models trained on the optimized dataset by 0.1332 in terms of mean average precision. Moreover, this high standard of performance is achieved across multiple cultural contexts. Additionally, a model trained on a custom dataset achieves comparable results to those obtained with horizontal attention modules, indicating that culture-specific data is a crucial component for developing effective prohibited items detectors. This expertise can be applied to detect illicit non-X-ray items by substituting X-ray images with camera photos. In this context, a model scores 0.8375 in terms of mean average precision on the custom Real-World X-ray Valuation Dataset. The primary objective of Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves determining the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Advances in deep learning, specifically utilizing BERT, have led to significant progress in this area, with several strategies being developed to incorporate contextual information for sensitive words whose meanings remain constant across varying situations.  However, there is a major limitation to relying solely on context for disambiguation, given that words with inconsistent meanings may still be understood when isolated, as seen in the gloss approach.  To address this issue, we propose a novel framework that combines the context and gloss of a word to enhance the disambiguation process.  This proposed framework outperforms the current state-of-the-art models by achieving a 3.81% improvement in the overall WSD performance.  Furthermore, our model demonstrates superior performance when compared to traditional machine learning techniques, such as supervised learning, and equally competes with state-of-the-art Tagger models in terms of accuracy.  We also examine the effect of using both context and gloss information for words with inconsistent meanings and find that our proposed framework yields a 12.5% improvement in the WSD accuracy in such cases.  Finally, our model achieves a notable 4.11% improvement in the WSD task when the word sense ambiguity is relatively high.  To validate the effectiveness of our proposed framework, we conduct a human evaluation, and the outcomes corroborate the model's performance by indicating a 91% agreement with the human annotations.  We believe this achievement to be notable as nearly all previous studies on WSD utilized automatically generated datasets, whereas our proposed framework is evaluated using both human-generated and automatically created datasets. This paper tackles the challenge of encoding database names as symbols, a problem that limits the effectiveness of cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing. To overcome this, we propose a novel approach that leverages a supportive task to enhance paragraph representations with semantic information, allowing for more accurate identification of database symbols. By drawing on pre-trained models and utilizing a dual-task cross-domain training method, we demonstrate that our approach excels in incorporating semantic knowledge from natural language text, resulting in improved performance on both text-to-SQL parsing and semantic analysis tasks. Notably, our method achieves exceptional results when compared to baseline models that rely on superficial patterns, and our code is publicly available for review and replication. Additionally, we introduce the CodeSearchAsia Dataset, a large-scale cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing dataset that contains over 300,000 examples, alongside accompanying database files, for further research and development. This dataset holds significant potential for advancing code search and natural language program generation techniques. 

In code search, our approach outperforms state-of-the-art models like Low-Cross and Reduce-Unnecessary-Labels by marginally improving the mean average precision metric from 24.5% to 25.4%, and significantly reducing errors by 1.4, while increasing the mean reciprocal rank by 0.04 on the CodeSearchAsia Dataset. These gains translate to higher accuracy rates on actual database retrieval tasks, as evaluated through manual code searching, and our results suggest that high precision code searching, defined as above 0.95, can be achieved for at least 45% of searches with only 10% of the typical search budget required. Notably, our code searching outcomes also reveal distinct patterns for (a) frequent single-word searches, (b) multiple-word searches with clear syntax, (c) semantic searches that match several clauses, and (d) ambiguous searches with no clear matches, and our analysis indicates that nearly 80% of all code searches fall into the first category. 

On the text-to-SQL parsing task, our approach excels in accurately identifying the best single table schema out of up to 150 options with only a 5% error rate, compared to 15%, while reducing errors by half and achieving a 10% higher precision rate on actual database population tasks, as evaluated through manual data entry. Additionally, our method successfully handles a wide range of semantic combinations, including both simple and complex queries, and our analysis of code searches uncovers several key patterns that could guide the development of more effective natural language program

This approach, which is based on a random phase-space ensemble averaging method inspired by the Toulouse-Ginzburg decomposition, effectively separates the hydrodynamic and nonhydrodynamic modes of the system. As a result, the hydrodynamic modes are governed by simple universal equations that are similar in form to those found in classical hydrodynamics, but with additional nonequilibrium fluctuations and correlations. Furthermore, this new approach enables the development of a robust and flexible theory for describing the dynamics of interacting Bose gases, which includes situations where interactions are finite-range or long-range, and even applies to superfluid black holes in the gravitational regime. Using this approach, a broad spectrum of nonequilibrium phenomena can be studied, and it has already shown promise in describing the nonstationary behavior of interacting Bose gases through both numerical solutions and approximate analytical estimates. Temporal activity detection is a sub-task of video annotation that identifies the start and end times of explicit activities. A major challenge lies in processing contextual events that occur both before and after the target activity, which can significantly impact detection results. Contextual events that happen after the activity of interest may be particularly difficult to incorporate, as they can hinder the segmentation process by introducing unnecessary complexity. A notable approach called Dual-Context-Agnostic Network is proposed to address this issue by learning context information relevant to the activity's onset and continuation. By doing so, this method is expected to enhance the detection of temporal activities by modeling contextual events affecting the activity's onset and disappearance, in addition to those that influence its middle sections. A comprehensive evaluation of the proposed method is conducted by applying it to the specific task of fall detection, a challenging activity that is not easily detectable through traditional methods. The proposed network is then tested on a large sports video dataset, and its results are compared to state-of-the-art techniques like Dual-Context-Agnostic Network and other approaches like ActivityNet and TARTINO. The proposed method is found to outperform these techniques on all evaluation metrics, indicating its superiority. The code for the proposed method is made available online for consideration by the community. A further analysis is conducted to identify key factors that contribute to the method's effectiveness, and several potential extensions are suggested for future improvement. Intelligent agents are increasingly being used in educational settings, reflecting the broader trend of using multi-agent systems to solve complex problems. The need for a robust and adaptable knowledge base in these agents has led to the development of various knowledge acquisition methods, including the instructor-pupil framework, which has become a prominent approach in recent years. This article provides an in-depth review of the instructor-pupil framework, exploring its key aspects, such as the types of relationships used, search strategies, and methods for updating the knowledge base, as well as discussing potential applications and future directions for research. Additionally, we outline potential extensions to the framework and highlight the need for more rigorous evaluation methods in this domain. Furthermore, we propose a new label for this technology, suggesting that the term "student-agent framework" more accurately reflects the involvement of multiple pupils in the learning process. This review aims to serve as a foundation for further research into the student-agent framework, encouraging developers to share their knowledge and expertise in this field. This research uncoveres a universal relationship governing the location of these transitions as mapping frequency changes, a phenomenon observed in polymer networks, living cells, and various other systems. Furthermore, our findings reveal that the size of the shear-augmentation regime follows a precise temporal pattern, indicating an essential property of dynamic systems that undergo transitions in response to external forces. Additionally, we demonstrate that the elasticity within the shear-augmented state contributes significantly to the temporal scaling of the transition's size. This research may lead to a better comprehension of the intricate relationships between viscoelasticity, structure, and function in complex systems across various scales and contexts. A question that has been debated is whether current search engines, like Google's Web search, are susceptible to the same type of bias and limitations that can influence other information retrieval systems. To address this inquiry, we designed an experiment to examine the impact of Google's customization on the effectiveness of its search results. We focused on identifying relevant information that may be hidden from users due to the customized presentation of search engine results. Unlike previous studies which measured the overall accuracy of search engine outcomes, we based our evaluation on a more direct method by comparing the results of a comprehensive search that retrieves all pertinent information with the outcomes of a customized search that only displays a limited number of results. Our data reveals that a substantial amount of pertinent information may be overlooked when searching through customized search engine results. Furthermore, we discovered that the percentage of missed information is significant, at least in our domain of study, which was the topic of searching for full-text information. Additionally, we found that the percentage of missed information varies depending on different search aspects, or topics, which could have implications for researchers who aim to evaluate the efficacy of search engines in a controlled manner. We believe that our results hold important implications for any system that relies on automated ranking of information, and we conclude by outlining potential avenues for further research into this topic. Additionally, we provide concrete suggestions for methodological approaches that could be employed in future studies. These proposed methods could facilitate a more in-depth examination of the bias that is inherent in the automated ranking of information, which is a topic that was first introduced by a seminal study in 1990. That groundbreaking research introduced the concept of "precision as a function of number of documents retrieved," which we refer to as the traditional approach. We also outline two novel methods for measuring the effectiveness of information retrieval systems, and we anticipate that these methodological approaches will be useful for studying any system that utilizes automated ranking to present retrieved information to users. Lastly, we express our hope that our study, along with the proposed methods, will contribute meaningfully to the ongoing discussion and research into the topic of bias in information retrieval systems. That discussion and research is crucial because information retrieval systems are fundamental tools that are used extensively across multiple domains, and any limitations or bias in these systems has far-reaching implications for users in those domains. That is why we used a rigorous experimental design, along with rigorous analysis and validation techniques, to study this critical topic. Our study produced significant results, and we hope that these outcomes, along with the proposed methods, will make a valuable contribution to the discussion

This research paper proposes a novel approach to developing controllers for complex nonlinear control systems prone to vulnerabilities in their input signals. Specifically, it outlines the design of an controller that can ensure a specified safe reaching point for a system in need of control, provided that the system's input limitations are linear or positively correlated with the system's state. A new theoretical concept, known as the Input Limited Control Barrier Function, serves as the basis for this approach and is defined through the use of transversality conditions similar to those found in Control Barrier Functions. Finally, an illustrative example demonstrating the effectiveness of this method in a transportation context is presented. Additionally, the paper outlines potential expansion paths for its core theory, specifically regarding the relaxation of its current limitations and the exploration of analogous solutions in the domains of observation limitations and constraints. Two appendices are included with further explanatory content and a key proof for the controller's viability theorem. To compare geometric shapes, a suitable comparison framework must be established independently of their orientation and location within the coordinate system. The CF-approximation framework successfully achieves this by dividing the coordinate system into equal squares and evaluating the area of shapes based on the number of squares they occupy. However, this method is only applicable when approximating closed curves and distinct shapes within a fixed area. To expand the CF-approximation framework's utility, a new method is developed to represent complex regions of the geometric shapes by assigning unique identifiers based on their CF-approximation areas. This approach combines the effectiveness of both approximation and accuracy, enabling easier comparison and analysis of shapes despite orientation and position variations. As a result, this method demonstrates substantial performance improvements over traditional approaches in both speed and efficiency. To demonstrate its utility, the developed system is applied to real-world imagery, showcasing its potential for shape analysis and image recognition applications. To evaluate the effectiveness of software metrics in predicting failure, a technique called paired permutation examination (PPE) is employed by various studies. Despite its utility, PPE lacks a clear methodology and reliable tools to perform comprehensive tests. To address this limitation, we propose an enhanced approach called precise paired permutation examination (PPPE) that builds upon existing techniques. Our method incorporates a statistical strategy and utilizes efficient computation methods to accurately assess the significance of certain predictions. We also introduce the design of a reliable tool, called pppe-tool, that executes complex PPPE tests efficiently. Our results demonstrate the superiority of our approach and tool by conducting a thorough analysis of seven widely used metrics against a diverse set of software systems. Our analysis shows that our tool can determine the predictive validity of certain metrics with a high degree of accuracy, significantly improving the assessment of their effectiveness. Furthermore, we investigate the predictive validity of submodules within software systems, demonstrating the potential for improved results. Our analysis also reveals the importance of selecting appropriate metrics for specific types of software, as well as the need for further research on predicting software vulnerabilities. Our study and results are supported by an excellent pppe-tool, that is available at https://github.com/PPPE-SRC. A well-known dimensionality reduction technique called CountSketch employs randomized linear measurements to map vectors into a lower-dimensional space, particularly effective at identifying the top elements (with the largest squared magnitude) of a given vector. However, the CountSketch sketch falls short in situations where the querying vectors rely on feedback from previous queries. In such scenarios, the classic estimator can be manipulated by vectors that appear halfway through the querying process, but only if the sketch uses the standard linear estimator. In a novel development, our research reveals that when the counting functions within the sketch exhibit a specific property, the estimator becomes resilient to manipulations, even in situations where the querying vectors adapt following previous outcomes. Furthermore, we demonstrate that no counting function possessing this property can achieve similar results. In addition, we introduce a new estimator that efficiently mitigates the risk of manipulation, achieving an estimate whose squared error is comparable to that of an ideal non-adaptive estimator. Our research also extends to settings where the querying vectors form an orthonormal basis, and we explore connections to other dimensionality reduction techniques. Overall, our findings enhance our understanding of the CountSketch sketch and its variants, valuable for any application relying on randomized linear measurements, such as linear solvers, least squares, and various machine learning algorithms. Our work is complemented by a dedicated supplementary material section. Additionally, we would like to express my gratitude to the reviewers for their invaluable feedback, which has been incorporated into the final version of this manuscript. In conclusion, our research lays the groundwork for exploring other contemporary dimensionality reduction techniques with highly adaptable targets. A recently proposed relation connecting a material's transport entropy to its average energy and number of particles is tested for a vortex fluid using the Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer model. To apply this test, a new expression for the vortex fluid's chemical potential is needed, and this is achieved by equating the change in its free energy to the change in its entropy. These results significantly surpass previous discoveries and contribute to a deeper comprehension of the Standard Model. Moreover, they establish benchmarks for further research in the coming decades. Soft-tissue alignment, a complex task due to tissue deformability and variability, is a crucial step in medical image processing, particularly in oncology and surgical planning. Existing methods often struggle to accommodate the biases inherent in medical image analyses. We introduce a novel non-rigid surface-based alignment technique that leverages external shape information to facilitate efficient and bias-minimized registrations. By representing organs as dynamic, gravity-driven shapes, we minimize a cumulative energy function combining boundary matching terms and elastic properties, using a PDE system that simplifies solution seeking. This approach not only reduces bias but also exploits tempering and coarse-grained versions of the elasticity term, enabling scalable solutions and capturing short-scale details. We validate our method against multiple benchmarks, demonstrating its capacity for both clean and noisy data, multi-component analyses, and comparisons against established methods like Demons and B-spline based approaches. Furthermore, we apply our technique to real-world tumor measurements, achieving accurate within-patient registrations and demonstrating its potential as a cancer progression model. Software and data are available at https://github.com/allemand/med-registry-demo and https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1xQrLQD1JL2lgG2KZK0kQbQJpTbGjLZLQ. Additionally, we include an open access video at https://drive.google.com/file/viewer/fileId?id=1xQrLQD1JL2lgG2KZK0kQbQJpTbGjLZLQ. Specifically for bias evaluation, we utilize real-world data combined with the EBI Model, a widely accepted soft-tissue biomechanical model, as reference shapes. These references are derived from combined MRI-CT data, used to define organ boundaries and elastic properties, which we incorporate into our registration process.
