In contrast to general purpose processors, Neurofluid Hardware (NPH) and Neuromorphic Core (NC) adapters specialize in efficiently executing extensive neural network tasks by minimizing idle time and system energy consumption. However, these specialized processors still waste resources by processing individual neural network input values separately. To overcome this limitation, we propose the development of a Neural Network Categorizer that uses Spiking Random Neural Networks. This innovatory module refines and refines input data before it's fully processed, ultimately resulting in optimized use of NPH and NC resources. We test our model's capabilities as a prototypical example using a Spiking Neural Network implementation of a multiclass classifier, revealing a notable boost in accuracy and a substantial reduction in energy consumption. Compared to standard neural network methods, our results show a 23% improvement in categorization speed and a 27% decrease in energy consumption when using NPH, along with a 21% increase in speed and a 25% decrease in energy consumption when using NC. Additionally, our model achieves 93% of the same accuracy as traditional methods with only a 7% increase in training time. We also explore different optimisation techniques and find that our model's performance can be further enhanced. We believe our revised version holds significant potential for application in vast dataset categorization. Furthermore, we examine the feasibility of integrating a Neural Network Categorizer with a Super Resolution application using a biologically plausible large-scale Spiking Neural Network. Although the project overshoots current processing capabilities, it paves the way for the development of a next generation of Neurofluid Hardware that integrates categorization and learning functions in a single, highly efficient platform. Active galactic nuclei (AGNs) offer a chance to investigate particles with masses significantly smaller than a proton, potentially providing answers to fundamental questions about the universe. Recent research into the spin values of massive AGNs has yielded surprising results, with findings that do not align with standard stellar evolution models. Rather than assuming these results are anomalous, we decide to reexamine the relationships between the spin values of AGNs, the ultralight bosons that may reside within them, and the process of superradiance. By applying a method known as Bayesian statistics, we determine the likelihood of ultralight bosons exhibiting either single particle or ensemble behavior given the spin values of these AGNs, and find that single particle behavior is a significantly better fit to the data (by a factor of approximately 125) than ensemble behavior. We describe the objectives of the TESS-Keck Survey in detail, focusing on determining the size of small planets and identifying potential targets for the TESS Continuous Viewing Zones. Additionally, we outline the target selection process, taking into consideration factors such as planetary systems of interest, host stars with minimal astrophysical noise, and candidates with ambiguous planet dimensions. From the initial 855 candidates, our survey shortlisted 59 planets spanning 12 systems for further analysis using Keck/NIRC2. These targets exhibit a wide range of planet sizes, including small rocky worlds and larger gas planets, with several being potential targets for CVZ observations. Our analysis indicates that 27% of these planets are subject to inaccuracies greater than 50%, with all but one being small planets; 13% of the targets have inaccuracies exceeding 100%, with most of these also being small planets. Our strategy for observing these targets involves selecting planets with anticipated dimensions greater than 1.2 to 1.5 times the Earth's size, depending on various factors including stellar type and planetary system characteristics. If the dimensions of these planets are indeed larger than expected, it could imply a more gradual planary size distribution trend, consistent with observations from NASA's Kepler and TESS missions. Our survey also provides insight into the relationship between host stars and their planets, revealing a correlation between stellar mass and planetary sizes, as well as an increased likelihood of having multiple planets when the star has a low mass. The Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effect significantly impacts the rotational states of small asteroids by exerting a net torque resulting from solar radiation reflected and re-emitted by the surface. As a consequence of this phenomenon, the rotation period of these asteroids gradually changes, which can be measured through light curves as the YORP effect induces periodic variations. To determine the YORP-induced acceleration in three asteroids - (10115) 1992 SK, (1685) Toro, and (1620) Geographos - researchers analyzed their rotational states over time frames of up to twenty years with data from the All Sky Asteroid Photometric Survey and the Lincoln Near-Earth Asteroid Research project, incorporating constraints from magnetic field measurements for the (1620) Geographos analysis. Compared to computational models featuring appropriate parameters, the measured data showed a clear rotational acceleration in (10115) 1992 SK and (1685) Toro, as well as in (1620) Geographos at a much lower acceleration rate. These findings highlight the complex interaction between the YORP effect and the asteroids' physical properties, which can result in rotated mass unequal distribution, further supporting the theory that the (1620) Geographos double-axial rotation mode is likely the result of its unique internal structure. Moreover, this research pinpoints the computational models' capability to determine the YORP effect, a previously challenging task, by utilizing the traditional approach combined with light curve analysis. This method may be a useful path for investigating other asteroids with varying rotation periods. Additionally, this study suggests that (10115) 1992 SK and (1685) Toro could enter a state of chaotic rotation in the future, while (1620) Geographos is expected to require millions of years to experience a similar rotation change. This discovery may imply the presence of a substantial interior structure in (1620) Geographos, such as a solid core, which needs further validation through magnetic field measurements, meteorites, or JAXA's "Asteroid Impact and eX-explosion Detection" mission that will be launched in the mid-2020s. The youth in India are heavily influenced by social media, particularly Instagram, which they use to stay informed about politics. Understanding online political discussions on Instagram is vital to comprehending the views of this demographic. However, analyzing Instagram conversations poses a challenge due to the limited information available on connected conversations. To address this issue, we developed a novel approach for detecting and annotating related posts on Instagram, using a combination of machine learning techniques and Instagram-specific features. By applying this approach to a set of Indian youth, we collected a substantial dataset of online conversations and analyzed them from multiple perspectives, including the topology of retweet networks, influence spreading, and community discovery. Our results reveal intriguing aspects of online political discussions on Instagram, including the formation of hierarchical networks and communities that reflect distinct viewpoints, as well as the significant impact of influential users in disseminating information. Additionally, we observed a notable difference in online behavior between young Indians who are actively engaged in politics and those who are not, with the latter exhibiting temporary interest in politics that wanes over time. Our research provides valuable insights into the dynamics of online political discussions on Instagram, with implications for information spread, influence measurement, and community discovery, as well as potential applications in tracking online conversations and campaigning. Furthermore, we open-source our approach and associated data, along with our source code and visualization tools, to facilitate further exploration of these findings and the broader social media politics landscape. Additionally, we offer this as a starting point for research into other online discussions on Instagram and other topics. Finally, we highlight potential avenues for expansion, with a focus on incorporating additional features, users, and datasets. With this in mind, we invite the research community to build upon our work, with potential opportunities for collaboration and exchange. Our approach is composed of three primary components, namely online subgraph extraction, entity-based annotation, and feature engineering. We utilized these features to examine online discussions from various perspectives, including retweet networks, influence spreading, community discovery, and social network analysis. Our results reveal valuable insights into the conversations we studied, with implications for both academic research and practical applications. Furthermore, we emphasize the importance of handling personal data responsibly, with transparency and security as the top priorities. Our approach is well-suited for detecting and annotating connected conversations on other platforms as well, with Twitter expression studies being a potential area for exploration and extension. Additionally, we believe our approach can also be applied to studying online discussions within other domains, with Twitter being a prime example due to its widespread use and the substantial amount of data available

A comprehensive understanding of magnetic fields in cool stars is vital to assessing stellar evolution and astroseismology. However, current magnetic field measurements are limited to high-concentration fields in active stars and the exact characteristics of low-concentration fields remain unclear. To address this knowledge gap, a new dataset of 651 cool stars, featuring detailed ultraviolet spectral observations, is presented. By utilizing the CANONization of Ultraviolet Spectra, a tool that breaks down UV spectra into components resembling solar spectra, researchers can determine the elemental content, stellar temperature, surface gravity, and magnetic field strength for each star. This process is highly automated, allowing for a large number of stars to be analyzed efficiently. Validation of the method was performed on a subset of 125 stars with established field strengths, showing good agreement and accuracy. The resulting data reveal a continuous distribution of magnetic field strengths in both solar-like stars and M dwarfs, spanning up to 300 G. This dataset, referred to as the M-dwarf Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Collection, will provide valuable information for future studies of cool stars and aid in refining models of global stellar properties. Furthermore, this dataset can be utilized to identify the coolest stars suitable for exoplanet detection using transit lighting curves or spectroscopic radial velocity curves. By expanding the current understanding of low-concentration magnetic fields, this study contributes to a more comprehensive picture of stellar evolution and will aid in optimizing the selection of suitable cool stars for exoplanet detection. The full dataset is available on the TEFF and LOGG website: https://www.tefflogg.org/data/mdusccoolstars.html. This design produces a narrow bandwidth and a significant increase in the relative bandwidth in the negative order. Numerical analysis demonstrates that a line wave with a 1% bandwidth and a 0.76% relative bandwidth can be obtained with a simple design, or a line wave with a 3% bandwidth and a 1.85% relative bandwidth using a design that incorporates a deflection layer. The line wave's characteristics can be adjusted through the length of the microstrip. Furthermore, full-scale simulation confirms that a line wave with a 2% bandwidth and a 1.3% relative bandwidth can be achieved using a dual microstrip structure. This design facilitates the creation of line waves with high frequency separation and low loss, making it suitable for applications such as optical frequency multipliers and optical isolators. The proposed structure can also be modified to support line waves with distinct frequencies in close proximity. The analysis reveals that the proposed metastructure supports line waves with low loss, high frequency separation, and minimal coupling between the two lines. The radiation resistance is maximized when the distance between the microstrips is equal to the width of a single microstrip. Within complex suspensions, particles can exhibit multiple types of interactions that govern how they interact with forces, either repelling or attracting other particles. Depending on these interactions, certain particles may serve as pullers, responding to forces by moving towards them, while others act as pushers by moving away from applied forces. Depending on the dominant type of interaction, some particles may also remain unaffected by applied forces, serving as non-reactive observers. This particular scenario can result in multiple combinations of these responses across different particles, leading to pairing scenarios such as a puller and a pusher, or multiple pullers or pushers. However, one particular combination remains unexplored - that of two pullers. In this study, we successfully demonstrate the discovery of this hidden configuration by training a neural network to identify patterns of force response in a suspension consisting of two types of interacting particles. By applying machine learning algorithms to analyze the patterns of force response in a random mixture of pushers and non-reactive particles, we found that they failed to detect the presence of two pullers. In contrast, a distinct two-puller state was uncovered when analyzing mixtures composed of pushers and pullers. In addition, we observed that the two-puller state could also emerge spontaneously during simulations of interacting particles, and we investigated the dynamics that govern this particular configuration. Furthermore, we explored how this hidden state could be extracted from noisy data, and we investigated the spatial distribution of particles within the two-puller state by incorporating simulation-based data into our machine learning model. Our research uncovered novel insights into the dynamics of complex suspensions and demonstrated the potential of machine learning to accelerate and enhance simulations of interactive particles. Additionally, our findings can benefit different applications such as designing materials with controlled response to forces and better understanding the behavior of biological cells that rely on complex interactions with external forces. Finally, our research showed that machine learning can provide valuable insights even into seemingly simple systems like a suspension of interacting particles, and we hope this study will motivate investigation into other complex systems through similar approaches. The effectiveness of reinforcement learning in robotics is significantly limited by its reliance on explicit rewards, which can be difficult to obtain. This challenge prompts the development of a methodology that focuses on constructive feedback, which is inherent in statements like "move more" or "turn less." This approach, called the Constructive Feedback Procedure (CFP), combines reinforcement learning with active hypothesis testing to efficiently discover optimal actions by asking and answering questions about action effects through constructive feedback. Our CFP framework addresses several key issues related to constructive feedback, including how to interpret it, what questions to ask, and how to handle uncertainty. By leveraging the benefits of both reinforcement learning and active learning, CFP yields policies that minimize regret and achieve certain performance guarantees, even with noisy feedback, in environments that change over time. Our experiments showcase the superiority of CFP over alternative approaches, and it has potential applications in areas beyond robotics. The code for our experiments is openly available online. Our work also introduces the concept of conditionally dependent environments, which modeling multiple interconnected sub-environments through conditional dependencies, a topic that we explore in depth in a accompanying paper. This new framework, along with CFP, paves the way for the development of more complex systems from multiple simple systems by learning from constructive feedback in each one. This combined approach enhances the performance of our original CFP method, and it has been made available online for public access. Additionally, we introduce the RCL benchmark suite of multi-task learning problems defined using constructed feedback targets, along with our code for this benchmark. Continuous phase modulation detection using traditional non-coherent detection methods has historically been resistant to differential detection's performance gains. This discrepancy can be attributed to the reduced post-differentiation phase ambiguity of CPM signals. However, there are instances where the addition of differential detection is relevant, such as in applications where the transmission system's complexity needs to be minimized. This study investigates methods to increase the performance benefits obtained from differential detection by introducing additional signal processing delays in both detection branches, which counteracts the initial decrease in phase ambiguity. Simulation results, conducted across various CPM signals and modulation indices, demonstrate notable enhancement of up to 3 dB in BER performance when using this approach. Furthermore, the findings suggest that as the modulation index increases, the optimal delay also tends to increase, which provides valuable guidance for system designers. Optimal differential detection performance gains are achieved with approximately 1 to 2 symbol periods of additional delay across medium to high modulation index ranges, which may facilitate its adoption in certain applications. A common approach to addressing this issue involves first removing rain from the video,
then generating the new frames to complete the circuit.

information and employ a flow-guided transformation to enhance the disentanglement
process.
Overall, our approach yields superior results for optical flow estimation and occlusion
detection compared to the current state-of-the-art methods. Moreover, our eliminated
frames exhibit a more realistic appearance and show improvement in video deinterlacing and
super resolution tasks. Unlike traditional methods that rely on policy iterations to evaluate rewards, our method utilizes human feedback to sort groups of trajectories into ranking orders based on their perceived reward values. Our experiment shows that Visually Supported Cluster Ranking reduces the time needed for reward learning by tenfold, resulting in policies that are twice as good as those obtained with optimal policy optimization methods. The Five Factor Model of personality has been widely accepted for categorizing individual personality traits. Recent research aims to integrate the Five Factor Model with the Research Domain Criteria (RDoC) to create a comprehensive framework that explains impulsive and addictive behaviors. This study builds upon this initiative by applying the Five Factor Model to a sample of 1,500 participants who used the Five Factor Adjective List to describe themselves. The data was subsequently analyzed using factor analysis to verify the model's applicability and assess the efficacy of its dimensions in predicting problematic drug use. Our research confirms the presence of the Five Factor Model in the data and discovers that certain personality traits are associated with increased risk of drug abuse. Notably, the results suggest that conscientiousness and agreeableness exhibit a non-linear relationship with drug use risk, with moderate levels being optimal, while extraversions and openness to experience display a linear relationship with an elevated risk of drug abuse. Our study contributes to the growing body of research that integrates the Five Factor Model with the RDoC framework and highlights the importance of considering personality traits when developing prevention and intervention programs for drug abuse. Additionally, the study provides a preliminary framework for assessing drug use risk that combines the Five Factor Model with the RDoC framework. This knowledge base consists of nearly 500,000 factual connections, such as "if a person eats a certain meal, they will probably feel full" or "if someone reads a book, they will likely learn something new." This paper examines the distribution of initial values in a specific range for uniform parking functions of length n. We derive formulas for the total number of uniform parking functions of length n with initial values in the range {1,...,k} or {1,...,n}, as well as the number of those with unique maxima, and provide a recursive approach for calculating the former. Our findings for the total count align with existing research, but we generalize it for initial value ranges. Specifically, for uniform parking functions of length n with initial values in the range {1,...,k}, if k n, the count is equal to the sum of (k-i) choose (n-i) for i = 0 through k-n, and if k >= n, the count is simply the sum of (k-i) choose (n-i) for i = 0 through k. We also explore the asymptotic behavior of this distribution as n and k both approach infinity, finding that the proportion of uniform parking functions with initial values in a given range {1,...,k} converges to a value related to the harmonic series, and that the specific initial values 1 and n are unique maxima indicators for k = 1 and k = n respectively, with a transition in between where multiple values achieve this distinction. This analysis provides a foundation for further study of asymptotic behavior in the realm of parking functions. Our methods also involve analyzing complementary sets of integers and using combinatorial arguments to establish relationships between various counts of parking functions. These approaches may be applicable in exploring other counting problems. Finally, we offer a name for a broader set of sequences that share many characteristics with parking functions, and suggest several open questions for further research. This harmonic series connection holds value on its own, even independently of parking function context. Additionally, we explore sum-and-product relationships between integers within a certain range, establishing a link between the count of uniform parking functions and a broader set of sequences, and show that this relationship results in the harmonic series when considering initial value ranges in parking functions. In 2001, the discovery of T-dwarf GJ 229B by Hubble Space Telescope was a significant breakthrough, offering a unique chance to study this cool dwarf in detail. However, initial estimates of GJ 229A's age and mass are now considered inaccurate and certain characteristics of the system remain unclear. Utilizing the APOLLO code, which employs a holistic method to combine observational and theoretical data for consistent solutions, we reexamined the GJ 229 system. By incorporating existing data and modeling the system's components, the code provided an improved understanding of the system. Specifically, our analysis indicates that the primary star, GJ 229A, has a surface temperature of around 3700 K, which is slightly higher than initially estimated. The two stars are also found to be relatively close to each other, at an average distance of 0.016 AU, with an orbital period likely extending beyond 80 years. Our study also shed light on the nature of the binary system, revealing that it exists within a narrow habitable zone and undergoes significant variations in their luminosity, ultimately classifying them as UV-flare candidates. Furthermore, our research provides an updated mass estimate for the substellar companion, GJ 229B, which is now reported as having a mass of 32.9 +/- 2.3 times that of Jupiter, confirming it as one of the largest known T-dwarfs in our galaxy. With an age ranging from approximately 5 billion and a small margin of error, GJ 229B's size is consistent with theoretical models of cool dwarfs undergoing natural shrinkage. Our study also explores the possibility of the system hosting additional planetary bodies or stellar companions but finds no concrete evidence, indicating that further research is needed to fully understand the composition and dynamics of the GJ 229 system. Utilizing the APOLLO code to analyze this system also paves the way for applying the same method to study other binary systems that contain a main-sequence star and a cool dwarf in our galaxy. With advanced telescopes and the ability to obtain more precise data, our research provides a foundation for a deeper examination of the GJ 229 system and its components. Additionally, our study highlights the importance of incorporating theoretical models and existing data equally in scientific analysis to ensure accurate solutions, a principle that the APOLLO code embodies through its unique approach. With its distinctive method, the code offers a valuable resource for researchers that can help resolve complex issues and provide a better understanding of complex systems

Our research focuses on the interconnection between jet energy loss and the quark-gluon plasma's viscoelastic properties. Initially, we examine jet behavior within a linear viscoelastic medium, utilizing both hydrodynamic and solid-like approximations to model jet interaction. In the case of the hydrodynamic model, we simulate jet behavior using both linear and nonlinear interactions. In the case of the solid-like model, we model jet interaction using a similar method to the hydrodynamic model, but with a linear approximation only. Our simulations reveal that a linear viscoelastic model results in reduced jet energy compared to a hydrodynamic model, while a solid-like model produces similar results to the hydrodynamic model in terms of jet energy distribution. Furthermore, we examine the effects of a solid-like model on the development of jet fragments, and investigate the relationship between jet radius and the occurrence of inelastic scattering events. We analyzed the overfitting phenomenon in neural networks and suggested a regularization technique that addresses it by enforcing a specific constraint on the neural network. This constraint requires the network to maintain consistent output patterns for identical input vectors, thereby preventing the formation of irrelevant patterns that can lead to overfitting. Specifically, we formulated a regularization method that imposes a Lipschitz continuous constraint on the neural network by aligning its weights with those of a perfect discriminator. This method effectively reduces the capacity of the neural network by limiting the magnitude of its output changes in response to small input variations. We demonstrated the effectiveness of this technique across multiple datasets and network configurations. Notably, our method achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art techniques like dropout and batch normalization, often outperforming them in certain cases. We attribute the improved performance of our method to its strict enforcement of a consistent pattern constraint across all input vectors. In contrast, dropout and batch normalization only consider specific input subsets, which can still lead to pattern distortion and increased complexity. We believe our method can enhance the robustness of neural networks and mitigate the limitations of optimization algorithms in preventing overfitting. We experimentally verify the relationship between our regularization method and network performance, showing that its effectiveness depends on the number of training examples relative to network parameters. When the number of examples exceeds the number of parameters, the network is trained in an overfitting regime, and our regularization method successfully mitigates this issue. However, when the number of parameters far exceeds the number of examples, the network is in an underfitting regime, and our regularization method can struggle to improve performance due to the limited number of examples available. We propose a framework that integrates our regularization method with optimization algorithms, achieving notable improvements in real-world applications. This framework relies on the knowledge of the network's input and output ranges, which can be obtained through a simple modification of the known gradient sign descent algorithm. This modified algorithm determines the exact boundary values for the Lipschitz constraint and significantly reduces the number of hyperparameter settings required. We experimentally validate the performance of this framework across multiple real-world scenarios, showing consistent improvements in real-world accuracy. These results demonstrate the potential of our regularization method to enhance the robustness of neural networks and mitigate the limitations of optimization algorithms in preventing overfitting. We believe this method can also promote the exploration of new research directions in neural network architecture and optimization. Specifically, we suggest investigating the integration of our regularization method with novel neural network architectures that enforce a Lipschitz continuous constraint, such as Fourier neural networks

In the context of therapeutic gameplay, establishing a foundation of core gameplay is crucial, as it serves as the underlying mechanism that motivates players to engage in repetitive actions to overcome challenges. This foundation, comprised of elements such as variable reward scheduling, challenge progression, and control agency, provides the necessary framework for a positive gameplay experience that catalyzes emotional release and physical recovery.

By incorporating elements like unpredictable rewards, gradually increasing difficulties, and a sense of mastery over in-game actions, therapeutic gameplay applications can leverage the psychological benefits associated with these mechanisms to facilitate a connection between the player and the game that promotes relaxation, reduces stress, and fosters a desire to continue playing.

However, simply incorporating these foundations without consideration for the broader gameplay context may lead to an inferior result, lacking the overall coherence and engagement essential for an effective therapeutic gameplay experience.

In line with this approach, our submission explores the integration of foundational elements of therapeutic gameplay within the context of a Recover app, designed to aid physical therapy by motivating users to adhere to recommended exercises and meditation practices. The app represents a practical implementation of this approach, leveraging variables reward scheduling, progressive challenge, and agency within control systems to create a compelling and engaging experience that catalyzes emotional release and motivates physical recovery. The app's design and development serve as a case study for the Recover framework, an open-source repository of code available for reference. The app has been successfully developed in collaboration with physical therapy experts and a designer, and is currently available for download from the Google Play Store and Apple App Store. The associated research paper is set to be presented at the Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI 2021). The Recover app's design and development have been supported by the University of Auckland's Research Office, the Royal Society Te Apārangi, and the Auckland Bioengineering Institute. Centering Theory (CT) has long been a prominent approach in identifying equivalence relationships between sentences. Despite its limitations, CT still holds value in syntactic research. This work reexamines the principles of CT through the lens of modern neural coreference resolution systems, aiming to understand if the labels assigned by these systems align with the centerings predicted by CT. By analyzing coreference resolution models trained on the BERT baseline, our study reveals that the labels assigned by these systems follow different patterns, which differ significantly from the centers predicted by CT. Additionally, we find that the diversity of centers assigned by human annotators is relatively low, indicating that coreference resolution models trained on large datasets can produce a high degree of variability in assigned labels, a phenomenon that may be influenced by the degree of neural network size. The findings of this study provide valuable insights into the functioning of coreference resolution systems and highlight the importance of carefully selecting neural network parameters, particularly when working with systems that assign centerings. A preliminary analysis of the effectiveness of these systems, using standard metrics, shows that they perform on par with state-of-the-art coreference resolution models, suggesting that CT-centered evaluations should be conducted in conjunction with standard assessment methods. We have devised two general algorithms for identifying whether a directed graph can be represented in an upward planar layout. This involves determining if a set of nodes can be arranged in an upward planar layout, without interfering with each other, based on specific connections between them. The first algorithm establishes a connection between such arrangements and a concept called "knot diagram," allowing us to utilize a vast library of pre-existing preclusions. However, this association holds only for graphs where nodes have distinct identities. To accommodate graphs with potentially identical node identifiers, we develop a more complex algorithm, drawing from a broader library of preclusions that considers the relationships between subgroups of connected nodes. Both algorithms can handle additional constraints, such as coloring requirements. Moreover, we demonstrate the efficacy of these algorithms in addressing several specific challenges, including removing isolated loops, merging nodes, and adding edges, thus proving their value in real-world applications. Finally, we discuss several open questions and potential extensions for these algorithms. Additionally, we make both algorithms and our research notes publicly available. In quantum field theories, the operator expansion at a given spacetime point is essentially a linear combination of local operators evaluated at that point, whose coefficients are determined by the correlation functions of the fields. For a scalar field, the operator expansion can be expressed as a sum over a series of creators of conformal primary fields, whose coefficients are precisely the correlation functions of the scalar field with itself. Similarly, the expansion for a conformal primary field can be defined as a sum over the creators of a scalar field with various conformal weights. However, the coefficients of the expansion for a conformal primary field hold more information than the corresponding correlation functions of the scalar field, as they are invariant under the action of certain differential operators. The relationship between the expansions for a scalar field and a conformal primary field is explored, revealing a specific pattern that can be utilized to derive a crucial identity connected to the conformal bootstrap equation. This identity is then applied to regenerate a key consequence arising from the combination of the holomorphic and anti-holomorphic bootstrap equations, which itself implies the Primo conjecture recently put forward by Cardoso, Cantrell, and Frolov. Furthermore, by examining the explicit spacetime dependence, a more comprehensive understanding is gained about the operator expansion for a scalar field, its implications on the conformal primary field, and their corresponding Casimir operators. The analogies and differences between the operator expansions for scalar and conformal primary fields is also highlighted, as is the case for the combinations of these fields. The analysis extends to the higher-dimensional analogues of these fields, revealing similar patterns in their operator expansions. The unique features of the operator expansions for higher-dimensional conformal primary fields stem from their expansions being limited to a single creator of a scalar field with a specific conformal weight, in contrast to lower-dimensional conformal primary fields, which have expansions that cover a broader range of conformal weights. The results obtained from the analysis of the operator expansions for these fields may provide valuable insights for further research in quantum field theories. The theoretical framework developed here is expected to be applicable across a wider class of models that incorporate the described field types, making it a useful tool for exploring their underlying structures and potential connections. To demonstrate the utility of this framework, the derived identity from the analysis is applied to solve a related correlation function problem. The rise of cloud computing and virtualization has revolutionized the way companies approach infrastructure management, enabling rapid scalability and efficiency. This advancement, however, introduces new challenges in monitoring the performance of virtual devices and detecting potential breaches of service level agreements (SLAs). Traditional approaches, characterized by a centralized model using a single monitoring system, prove insufficient due to their limited scalability and reliance on a single point of failure. In contrast, this research explores the potential benefits of utilizing peer-to-peer (P2P) technology to design a distributed system for SLA breach detection, leveraging the unique characteristics of P2P networks to improve performance, reliability, and scalability. Specifically, this research proposes a novel architecture based on a P2P overlay, along with a algorithm for identifying SLA breaches, and presents a computational framework for evaluating and comparing different P2P-based implementations. Although this research focuses on application in cloud computing environments, the concepts and ideas may also be relevant to other domains requiring distributed SLA breach detection. Two prototype implementations have been developed to demonstrate the feasibility of this approach, and a simulated evaluation case study is presented to illustrate the performance benefits of P2P-based distributed systems for SLA breach detection. In conclusion, this research provides a new direction for the development of scalable and robust monitoring systems, capable of handling complex systems and dynamic infrastructure environments. In addition, this approach may also facilitate cost reduction by eliminating the need for centralized monitoring systems and allowing for more efficient utilization of system resources. Furthermore, this research may contribute to the creation of innovative and dynamic SLAs that adapt to changing performance conditions, and even enable the development of new services levels that incorporate real-time system dynamics. In essence, this approach may empower the construction of monitoring systems that can adapt to the ever-changing landscape of modern cloud computing environments, and thereby unlock new levels of performance, efficiency, and scalability. In theory, this approach may also pave the way for the development of new monitoring system architectures that can handle complex system dynamics, and demonstrate that the traditional centralized model is indeed outdated. In fact, this research explicitly challenges other domain experts to explore the potential benefits of P2P technology for distributed SLA breach detection, and to contribute to the advancement of this exciting area of research. Furthermore, this research also presents an opportunity for the exploration of various algorithmic solutions to detect performance data anomalies within P2P networks, and for the development of novel techniques that can handle the complexity of system dynamics, as well as for investigating new methods for the conversion of performance data streams into meaningful performance metrics

Initially, this effect was considered a limitation to the performance of a well-designed ERL, however our findings suggest that it instead presents an opportunity for enhancing particle distribution through a process known as the "regenerative beam fragmentation instability". This process occurs when a specific combination of transverse modes within the cavity leads to the development of perturbations in the fill pattern, resulting in the generation of new mode combinations. Our studies reveal that the behavior of this process is highly dependent on the initial fill configuration, with implications for the selection of cavity modes in ERLs. This discovery is of particular significance for the development of multibeam ERLs, where the interaction between different fill configurations may give rise to a wider range of mode combinations, making it essential to thoroughly assess this process through detailed particle simulations and experiments. Our research also highlights the value of carrying out cross-between-experiment validations, an aspect that is particularly important in the field of ERLs. Ultimately, a deeper understanding of this process is crucial for optimizing the performance of multibeam ERLs. The Southern Atlantic rift system exhibits asymmetrical geometry, with Africa breaking apart at a slower rate than South America.  Analyzing gravity and magnetic data from the southern Atlantic, the Runcorn and Bullard (1956) study identified the Omorfo Line, also known as the 2000 km long Rio Grande Rift System, separating continental blocks in the region.  This system consists of several parallel NNE-trending faults, primarily observed in seismics, and is characterized by low gravity anomalies and magnetic quiet zones.  Classified as a left-lateral shear zone, it controls the width of the South American-African continental margin.  It exhibits varied ages, with estimates ranging from 100 to 500 million years, based on different interpretations of geophysical data.  However, it is evident that it has been active during multiple phases of the South Atlantic expansion.  The Omorfo Line shows significant curvature near the Walvis Ridge, where it makes a sharp right turn, and this section of the rift system has experienced significant shear strain.  This shear strain is thought to have contributed to the formation of the distinctive V-shaped feature known as the Rio Grande Depression.  The Omorfo Line regains its original curve north of the Rio Grande Depression, and this section is where it exhibits the greatest curvature rate, with a value of 0.75 degrees per million years.  This high curvature rate is remarkable, as it is far greater than any other continental shear zone, and it suggests that this region has experienced significant extensional deformation.  This increased curvature rate results in faster break-up rates in South America compared to Africa, which can be attributed to an asymmetrical distribution of heat flow, with higher values in South America.  This difference in heat flow likely causes an increase in the strength of the African lithosphere, leading to slower break-up rates in Africa.  Additionally, this heat flow distribution may influence post-break-up evolution and the formation of passive continental margins in the region.  It is proposed that this line should be referred to as the Rio Grande Shear Zone, reflecting its active role in the expansion of the South Atlantic.  This name change also highlights the need for a revised model of the region, one that accounts for the shear strain experienced by the Omorfo Line during the break-up of the continent.  This revised model should incorporate map view velocity gradients and shear strains, with reference to the Euler pole, to provide a clearer understanding of this complex geological feature. Specifically, high temperature leads to random grain growth, medium temperature yields pinpointed epitaxy, and low temperature results in epitaxial layers that retain their mobility and unique crystal structure even after cooling down to room temperature. Notably, the optimal temperature for pinpointed epitaxy varies significantly depending on the Heusler material, which holds implications for the activation energy of surface atoms during the epitaxial process. Ultimately, this discovery paves the way for the fabrication of high-quality Heusler materials through epitaxy. Additionally, our findings may also extend to other layers that share structural and compositional similarities with Heusler materials. A primary challenge in learning from positive labels arises from their inherent ambiguity, rendering them insufficient for effective instance extraction in multi-label situations. Our proposed approach tackles this problem by utilizing a single given label in conjunction with a label set to extract instances that share the same attributes as the given label. Our method is mathematically expressed through a multi-label instance extraction network (MLIEN) framework, which incorporates a label distribution function to differentiate between distinct labels and alleviate the inherent ambiguities in positive labels. Moreover, we introduce a novel multi-label instance extraction algorithm (MLIGA) based on optimistic approximations and sorting techniques to identify instances that accurately capture the characteristics of each individual label. Our experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate the efficacy of our MLIGA in comparison to existing baselines and a specially designed biased benchmark, which we introduced to evaluate MLIEN. Our study provides valuable insights on the MLIGA framework, its limitations, and possible areas for future research. By introducing a new open-source framework called MultiLabelInstanceExtractor, we facilitate reproducibility and usability for both researchers and practitioners. Our study also explores the application of MLIGA in a real-world setting, where we improve the performance of a commercial recommendation platform. Our study is a pioneering effort on multi-label instance extraction, a significant research area with numerous potential applications, and we anticipate it to contribute significantly to its growth. As this parameter shrinks, the equation behaves like the traditional Allen-Cahn equation. Despite the decay, the energy of the solutions actually increases with time in certain cases, challenging the common assumption found in whole-space analyses. However, a more substantial advancement discovered in this research is that the energy possesses an upper limit that diminishes over time. This advancing limit continues to shift inward as time passes, forming a moving boundary that separates the solutions that reach the limit from those that do not. Numerical simulations are also provided to visualize and support these theoretical findings. Additionally, this study extends the analysis to a modified time-fractional Allen-Cahn equation, demonstrating that the observed behavior applying to the critical case also occurs for other subcritical energies. The source of gamma-rays in nearby galaxies emitting radio waves remains a mystery.  Hadronic emissions from the disks around black holes or supermassive compact objects might provide a possible explanation, especially if the disks are confined by magnetic fields that prevent gas and particles from escaping due to gravity, as suggested by research on magnetically captured disks.  By assuming that the gamma-ray emissions originate from these captured disks, we used data from Fermi and EGAD to identify 17 galaxies showing significant gamma-ray emissions.  Analyzing their magnetic field strengths, we found values ranging from 0.4 to 4 Gauss, which are comparable to the magnetic field strengths found in the magnetic fields surrounding black holes and the disks they orbit.  Interestingly, there is a clear correlation between these magnetic field strengths and the gamma-ray powers, indicating that high-energy gamma-rays in these galaxies could indeed be attributed to hadronic processes triggered by magnetic fields.  Furthermore, we found that the orientation of these magnetic fields can be deduced from the optical polarization, providing a new method for detecting magnetic fields in active galaxies across the universe.  This discovery also offers a means to study the physics of magnetic fields in astrophysical environments through multi-wavelength observations of nearby galaxies.  By exploring this further, we can expect to gain a deeper understanding of the processes occurring in these galaxies and their potential to produce high-energy gamma-rays.  This concept may also shed light on the long-standing mystery surrounding gamma-ray emissions from the center of our own Milky Way.  In addition, it could provide a framework for predicting magnetic field strengths in other active galaxies, which in turn can be used to assess the likelihood of hadronic processes occurring in these galaxies, ultimately producing high-energy gamma-rays. This study seeks to enhance the yield curve construction method, specifically the method known as the intermediate method or method three, which estimates yields for individual portfolios. Researchers divide the market into three sectors based on the Cobb Douglas production model and estimate the intermediate method's stage I parameters. These estimates are then used to map individual portfolios to a specific sector, effectively determining their yields. A key advantage of this approach is that it minimizes estimation errors and maintains confidentiality in line with the Cholesky decomposition method. Additionally, this approach facilitates forecasting portfolio yields by simply estimating the underlying factor yields. A key finding of this study is that prices and returns follow a joint Gaussian distribution, enabling value-based portfolio selection and cross-sectional yield prediction through the intermediate method. This approach outperforms the benchmark model in terms of precision and risk. A notable result of this study is the discovery of a strong positive correlation between the intermediate method's stage I parameters and the market portfolio's beta, bond price, and return volatility. This study provides evidence supporting the intermediate method's use in estimating individual portfolio yields. A limitation of this study is the lack of data for certain portfolios, particularly those holding bonds. Consequently, the study recommends further research on bond holding portfolios. Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and pyelectrophonocardiogram (PECG) offers a visual approach for analyzing heart sounds. Our proposed method for extracting features and classifying sounds as normal or abnormal is an adaptation of a previous approach. We incorporate the effects of external noise and physical deformities on PECG readings by developing a data augmentation technique. This method enhances the diversity of our dataset without requiring additional physiological measurements. We apply a convolutional neural network (CNN) to the augmented data and achieve a high accuracy rate of 99.13%, outperforming previous results. Furthermore, our model's performance is comparable even with limited data, indicating its potential for clinical applications. We publicly release our augmented dataset featuring sounds under external noise and physical deformities. This milestone marks the first time such varied data has been made available for PECG research. Our study paves the way for further advancements in heart sound classification to detect conditions like arrhythmia, valve disorders, and congestive heart failure. We anticipate future research to focus on analyzing complex sounds, identifying specific sound types, and developing models for real-time classification. Additionally, we intend to explore new features and classification approaches for comparing and validating results across different datasets. This study aims to establish a connection between various methods used to optimize portfolio performance through the enhancement of higher moments, including Value-at-Risk, Expected Shortest Time to Liquidation, and the Sharpe Ratio with fat-tailed errors. We demonstrate that minimizing both the VaR and ES is equivalent to optimizing the Sharpe Ratio with fat-tailed errors, and that ES can be viewed as a linear combination of VaR and the Sharpe Ratio with fat-tails. Furthermore, we show that the optimal portfolio for maximum diversity, represented by the variance of the optimal portfolio, is directly proportional to the inverse of the absolute value of skewness and kurtosis. Additionally, we establish that the optimal portfolio for the Sharpe Ratio with fat-tailed errors is linear in the parameters of the distribution. We validate our findings using real market data. Overall, our research highlights the complexity involved in optimizing portfolios that account for higher moments, and the variety of methods available to achieve this goal. Our analysis reveals that the choice of optimization method depends heavily on the specific characteristics of the distribution of asset returns. Finally, we investigate the issue of liquidity in portfolio optimization, introducing a new objective function that minimizes the expected time to liquidate assets and accounting for the costs incurred during the liquidation process. In the context of automated testing, software is automatically updated in response to new changes made to its underlying source code. Two techniques used for this purpose are dynamic test adaptation and virtualization of applications for testing. Our research focuses on overcoming common obstacles in these approaches by developing new methods for handling changes to software with virtual interfaces, as well as identifying and mitigating unforeseen consequences of modifications to the software's underlying code. These methods involve using static code analysis to pinpoint potential areas of concern and incorporate testing tools that detect both functional and performance issues in software. Our approach is illustrated through its application to a real-world system, a network management platform called Apache Airflow, for which we created a framework for adapting tests automatically in response to changes made to its Python code. The results of our research are available as an open-source repository that other researchers and developers can use as a benchmark. Furthermore, we explore potential directions for further expansion of our approach by automated testing tools, as well as the potential risks and benefits for software developers. The significance of our research is evaluated in terms of its achievements, the difficulties faced, and the lessons learned from the project. Finally, our approach is placed within the broader context of existing research on dynamic test adaptation and virtualization of applications for testing. The potential future advancements in this field are also considered, and the potential risks and challenges that future research may encounter. The project demonstrates the feasibility of automated testing for complex software systems with virtual interfaces, as well as the potential benefits and challenges associated with this approach. The findings of this research are applicable to multiple areas of software development, including big data, network management, and cloud computing. The project provides valuable insights for automated testing of additional software systems, as well as the potential risks and challenges associated with this approach. Recent findings suggesting that lepton-flavour universality is violated have sparked significant interest among physicists. To address this discrepancy, a class of extensions to the Standard Model has been proposed, involving Leptoquark particles in various forms. We explore the possibility that two specific Leptoquark particles, linked by a light flavor field, are created in a manner that violates lepton flavour, their masses being distinguishable. We demonstrate that in this scenario, producing these Leptoquarks in pairs results in a significant contribution to a particular anomaly-driven process that involves electrons, muons, and jets. Furthermore, we illustrate that this process can serve as a key signature for the Leptoquark pair creation, even when these particles undergo decay into heavier intermediate objects, such as charmed quarks. We also carry out a thorough analysis of the relevant production channels and decay pathways, showing that a substantial excess in events containing electrons and jets, along with muons and jets, can be found through a simple search algorithm at the Large Hadron Collider, even when the center-of-mass energy is as high as 14 TeV. The most pertinent production channels and decay modes yield distinct signatures that exhibit a notable peak around the predicted mass ratio of 1.035, corresponding to the flavor field mass. We find that the most powerful approach to detect these Uneven Leptoquark Duo Creation events involves a combination of a factor known as "k-factor" and the characteristics of events containing electrons and jets, alongside those containing muons and jets. We have undertaken a detailed numerical analysis for two distinct scenarios of these Leptoquark particles, with masses either both set at 1 TeV or both at 1.6 TeV, integrating up to 14 TeV in a range of 7 to 13 TeV in steps of 1 TeV. However, common time-series models struggle to handle high-dimensional data effectively, and the experts in the field typically require extensive domain knowledge to implement and fine-tune these models appropriately. In contrast, our proposed monitored learning framework, known as Temporal Series Monitored Learning, utilizes a simple and versatile base model that can process a variety of data types and forecast short-time periods. This approach leverages an efficient monitoring system that detects and rectifies data drift, selects the optimal model, and addresses missing values through prediction. Our results show that our method performs well compared to leading time-series competitors for life science data, and our case studies highlight the benefits of using it with real-world datasets from the PhysioNet challenge and the MIMIC-III database. Furthermore, our code is openly accessible on the GitHub repository https://github/TSMLein. Additionally, our study includes comprehensive comparisons with popular time-series models, such as Prophesy, Time Series Forecasting in Python, and Lighthouse, as well as the statistical controls used in monitored learning. In scenarios involving vectorlike compositeness, both the emergence of kinematic irregularities and anomalies in kinematic distributions can be explained by a single mechanism. Our analysis focuses on a particular scenario where a threshold for vector decay lies above most detected particles, making the decay process difficult to identify directly. As a result, we examine two approaches to interpret recent LHCb findings. Firstly, we assume that the threshold lies just above the detection limit, requiring a significant energy boost for decay product detection. In this case, both density irregularities in momentum space and distribution anomalies become less likely. However, we also consider the possibility that the threshold could be only slightly above the energy required for detection of decay products, which could plausibly result in the concurrent occurrence of both density irregularities and distribution anomalies. In this scenario, we demonstrate that current experimental data does not provide sufficient information to distinctly identify the vector's mass, composteness scale, or the magnitude of its coupling constant. Therefore, we anticipate future sensitive measurements of $B^0_s \to K^+ K^-$ observables to be crucial in determining the vector's properties and compositeness scale. Research articles typically present an overview of a topic, but they don't delve into details suitable for all readers. To gain a deeper understanding, users need additional information that exists elsewhere, but the difficulty lies in pinpointing exactly what more information is needed. Comprehension-driven summarization attempts to tackle this challenge by generating summaries that cater to a specific level of comprehension, as dictated by a knowledge source such as Wikipedia, thereby enabling users to grasp complex research concepts more effectively. While these summaries do incorporate more detailed information from the original articles, they also encounter an issue - they often include irrelevant information that needs to be filtered out. To address this, a dataset is introduced that consists of pairs of queries and responses, where each response is a summary of a specific aspect drawn from a background article. Both the queries and article backgrounds are sourced from Wikipedia, with the added benefit of eliminating any potential bias present in article writings. Additionally, two models are tested to evaluate their performance in generating these pairs of queries and responses. Ultimately, the evaluation of these models highlights the challenges they face, particularly the difficulty of determining the optimal level of comprehension, as well as the need to further examine the efficacy of these models through more rigorous means. In ASEP, particles move randomly through a lattice by exchanging places with adjacent counterparts, with an external drive that causes particles to shift towards the origin. Our research reveals that in ASEP with a remote drive, the velocity measure becomes a non-trivial, ergodic probability distribution that reflects spatial competition among particles. We investigated the semilocal neutron radius distribution, specifically its square, within both relativistic and non-relativistic mean field models. Our analysis revealed that the use of the baryon density in place of the neutron density in the contact term of the relativistic mean field theory leads to an overestimation of the neutron radius. Furthermore, a comparative study between different theories confirms that the variation in the neutron radius is largely confined to a narrow range. While the relativistic mean field theory generates a broader dispersion of neutron sizes, the non-relativistic mean field theory tends to concentrate on smaller values. We discovered that the average square radius of the neutron distribution is approximately 0.044 fm^2 in both frameworks. Notably, the standard definition of the neutron radius, obtained through the square root of the mean square radius, is not a gauge-invariant quantity. The effective use of solid catalysts in processes like partial oxidation, combustion, and gas-phase reactions depends heavily on their ability to manage heat. Effective heat transfer ensures that reaction temperatures remain stable, maximized, and safe. Despite its importance, the distribution of heat within a solid catalyst has not been thoroughly investigated. We utilized the principles of magnetic resonance imaging to examine the spatial heat distribution in a stationary bed of glass pellets probed using a rapid scanning technique. The resulting images and temperature readings showed that heat transferred deepest into the bed at around 0.5-1 pellet diameters, with further transfer occurring more slowly. This research provides valuable thermal management insights for optimizing the performance and safety of catalytic processes. The innovative imaging method we developed can be adapted for use with various types of heated beds, making it a versatile tool for investigating heat transfer in these systems. We also outline potential applications and extensions of this study to further exploration of catalytic processes and heat transfer in bed systems. The technique we used is based on nuclear magnetic resonance relaxation data and takes just a few seconds to collect, with no need for bed preheating. We compared this method with more conventional temperature measurement techniques, such as thermocouples, and it showed similar results in terms of spatial heat distribution. However, our method has several key advantages over these techniques, including the ability to obtain more precise temperature readings and a lower risk of measurement errors. We also examined how the thermal imaging technique works and its internal limitations, including how it measures temperature and the effects of bed inhomogeneities. We investigated the technique's performance with different types of heated beds, including those filled with pellets of a conductive material, but the results showed the same heat transfer patterns. The research raised some interesting questions about bed inhomogeneities and heat transfer, particularly in beds with large particles or those that become deformed during use, and it showed that thermal imaging can provide valuable insights to help with the design and optimization of catalytic processes. The technique also has the potential to be adapted for use with bed heating methods, such as fluid flow and electrical heating, and it could be applied to the study of heat transfer in various bed types, including those filled with ceramics, metals, and biological materials. We believe that combining thermal imaging with other techniques, such as spectroscopy and scanning electron microscopy, could provide a more comprehensive understanding of heat transfer and catalytic processes, and we anticipate that this research will be useful in the development of more efficient and safe catalytic processes. Both techniques aim to balance displacements and electrical potentials across subdomains by adjusting boundary conditions, and our study examines their potential as complementary methods for tackling complex heart muscle simulations. Our investigation reveals that balancing domain decomposition controls the balance gap and subdomain energy errors, and that tighter control results in greater accuracy but more significant computational costs. Our analysis indicates that Biebig-Düllmann-Otto's method offers a viable alternative to balanced domain decomposition, and that the choice of method depends on the level of accuracy and scalability required for a given application. Furthermore, we explore alternative control strategies and examine potential refinements to both techniques. Our research focuses on detecting privacy threats within biometric systems, specifically those using facial recognition technology. We've developed an analysis framework that utilizes machine learning and mathematical models to evaluate the privacy risks associated with circulating encoded facial images. This framework examines threat models, including the manipulation of facial images without detection by anti-synthesis systems, and includes a metric to measure the likelihood of such manipulation. We've also designed an experimental protocol to test the efficacy of our framework, and our results indicate that it can identify private facial images that likely evade detection by current anti-synthesis systems. Furthermore, our research reveals that there are significant differences in the level of privacy protection offered by various biometric standards and regulations. We conclude by discussing potential countermeasures to mitigate the threats to biometric systems and the importance of open-discussion among researchers, developers, and policymakers. Recent advancements in three-dimensional printing technology enable rapid manufacture of complex acoustic metamaterial structures. This letter showcases a novel approach to designing microacoustic metagratings in deep connection with a new class of acoustic metasurfaces, capable of manipulating sound waves at extremely high frequencies. By utilizing two-photon polymerization, we successfully created a microscopic metagrating in a millimeter-sized dimension, which shifts a plane wave by approximately 120 degrees at a frequency of 100 kHz. Our findings demonstrate that this type of structure can produce significant side-band gaps and localized resonance in extremely high-frequency ranges, making it potentially applicable for imaging inside the human body. This research lays the groundwork for further exploration of high-frequency acoustic phenomena and the development of new imaging technologies. Unlike conventional methods, two-photon polymerization allows for the instantaneous creation of complex acoustic metamaterial structures via laser light, enabling faster production of a wide range of metagratings and metastructures in comparison to traditional methods. Nevertheless, this technique still faces limitations in terms of size constraints, as demonstrated by the fact that a 360-degree metagrating remains unachievable with current methods. Furthermore, there is a need for further optimization of both two-photon polymerization and sol-gel nanostructuring methods to combine the advantages of both techniques. Ultimately, successful integration of these methods could pave the way for the creation of complex acoustic metastructures in an expedient and cost-effective manner. A significant amount of work remains to be done, however, before this technology can be applied to therapeutic applications that involve the use of high-power sound waves. Additionally, there are potential improvements to come from combining acoustic metagratings with photothermal effects in a process known as photoacoustic therapy. This letter provides a thorough explanation of a complex phenomenon known as a pump-probe dark fringe, which occurs when an acoustic metagrating is subjected to a sudden change and goes on to influence a range of related phenomena, including the creation of dark fringes in both reflection and transmission, the development of localized resonance, side-band gaps, and phase shifts. A fundamental understanding of this phenomenon is crucial for the development of new acoustic devices and components. This letter also introduces a new dimension to the study of acoustic metagratings through the use of two-photon polymerization, resulting in the creation of complex three-dimensional structures in the micro and millimeter range that can manipulate sound waves in this range. A recent study proposes a novel deep learning approach that utilizes generative adversarial networks to generate highly detailed flow velocity images from limited-resolution data in turbulent flows. A deep learning model was trained on and tested with high-resolution velocity data at different Reynolds numbers, specifically data with resolution ratios of 64^3 to 1024^3. The model demonstrated the ability to accurately reproduce high-resolution velocity images from lower-resolution images at the same and lower Reynolds numbers, even when the input images contained significant noise. Additionally, the model was able to produce accurate predictions for flows at Reynolds numbers it was not originally trained on. The predicted images were analyzed using laser Doppler velocity imaging and compared to actual measurements, showing a notable reduction in error, specifically a mean squared error of 2.5*10^-3 for the 64^3 to 512^3 resolution ratio. The model also demonstrated the ability to accurately reproduce surface vortex structures in flows with high viscosity. The proposed approach has the potential to enhance the resolution of flow velocity images in turbulent flows using only the images themselves, without the need for actual measurements at higher resolutions. This paper delves into the source of false positives in visual association detection tasks and proposes a new metric called Task-Related Positives (TRPs). We contend that TRPs represent a more desirable standard than traditional notions of positivity and propose a simple approach to focus on TRPs. Our approach involves applying a relevance filter to eliminate non-task-relevant detections before assessing accuracy. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by applying it to the VGG-Fish dataset, a commonly used dataset for fish recognition. Our results show that TRPs exhibit a more gradual decrease in frequency than traditional positives as we increase the accuracy threshold. This distinction becomes especially apparent at higher accuracy thresholds. Our research also investigates the influence of dataset quality on the performance of visual association detection models. We propose the idea of quantifying dataset quality based on the ratio of TRPs to total samples. Our approach demonstrates a range of desirable properties, including a clear improvement in average precision, a robust increase in the ratio of TRPs to total samples, and minimal degradation in precision. This report outlines the development of a novel Content Addressable Processor designed for concurrent programming, which has been effectively implemented on a Field Programmable Gate Array.  Unlike traditional Content Addressable Processors, our design excels at handling multiple program inputs simultaneously, while also providing a flexible means of program input that can be tailored to meet specific requirements.  Furthermore, our device utilizes a unique memory structure that combines the functionality of both fully interconnected arrays and cross-bar switches, allowing for optimal utilization of the available system resources.  Although designed for a simple FPGA architecture, our device demonstrates potential applicability to more complex systems, such as custom computing platforms and ASIC designs, with further optimization.  With a clock speed of approximately 100 MHz, our fully functional prototype has successfully executed a range of tests, indicating that our design is technically viable.  However, due to the fundamental differences between our design and traditional CAP architectures, comparative performance analysis is not feasible at this time.  On the positive side, our device offers enhanced concurrency capabilities, at the cost of increased difficulty in program development.  In recognition of these limitations, we are currently exploring adaptations of our design that could facilitate more straightforward programming approaches.  With further development and optimization, our content addressable concurrent processor is expected to become a highly efficient tool for executing complex computational tasks with high degrees of concurrency.  In the interest of fully disclosure, we must note that the design for our content addressable concurrent processor has been influenced by the ideas presented in the paper titled "Content-Addressable Microcode" however, due to the fact that publication date of that paper falls outside of the accepted timeframe, we are compelled to include this acknowledgement in the manuscript. A prominent court ruling in the United States case of In re Apple Inc., 857 F.3d 100 (2d Cir. 2017), involved the company refusing to cooperate with an FBI investigation, stating they couldn't access data due to an encrypted system. The court ultimately ordered Apple to assist the FBI in disabling the encryption feature. This paper delves into the implications of this ruling, considering the arguments presented by Apple and the government. We focus on the jurisdictional aspects, specifically whether a court can compel a third party to create or modify encrypted software. The paper presents two models representing this scenario and proves the complexity of determining an ordered decryption existence is co-NPC. Additionally, we identify an ordered decryption to exist under specific cryptographic protocols and show that a modification of one such protocol reduces the complexity from co-NP to NP under certain constraints. This research provides insights into potential policies governing third-party encryption and the implications of court orders on the encryption process. We discuss the standards of modern encryption and the potential for a "key escrow" system, concluding with an analysis of a protocol we term BC-Hash. We leave for further investigation the question of whether a court can compel a company to provide an unencrypted version of a message, for which we present an example of a protocol that likely meets this standard. This example, a hash function protocol based on BC-Hash, reduces the complexity of determining an ordered decryption existence to NP. We anticipate this result to also hold for more complex protocols standard in modern encryption, although a formal proof of this conjecture remains pending. In the context of the Apple case, we demonstrate that if the court had jurisdiction over Apple, but not the user who owned the encrypted device, ordering Apple to provide access to the data would have the same effect as compelling the user to cooperate. This conclusion holds for most practical applications and standard protocols, for which a formal definition of "practical applications" is provided. Finally, we note that the potential incorporation of unneeded data into an encrypted message may raise additional legal implications, for which a formal framework is proposed, involving a new protocol based on BC-Hash, for which a decryption existence proof is presented. This new protocol meets a higher standard of security, specifically one that could prevent the creation of covert messages, often referred to as an "oracle."
